speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, March 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government; and the amendment of Mr. Gray (Windsor West) (p. 17722).

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When debate ended on Friday, March 1, the hon. member for Surrey North had eight minutes remaining in debate, plus ten minutes of questions and comments.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to resume the debate I started on Friday concerning the cutbacks in the budget.
On Friday, I spent most of my time looking at the impact of the cuts to Established Programs Financing, particularly the impact it was going to have on our medicare system, which is now under grave threat from successive budgets by this government.
Today, I want to take a few minutes to talk about the Canada Assistance Plan, which again was a partnership between the province and the federal government. It was a partnership very much like medicare, in which the province and the federal government agreed to share 50 per cent, with the object of alleviating poverty and dealing with child abuse and neglect, and the causes thereof.
In most partnerships, the agreement is that both parties must agree before there are significant changes. However, we have seen in the last two years that this government has unilaterally decided it is going to abandon the concept of partnership with Canadian provinces and abandon the kinds of goals and aims that are set out in the Canada Assistance Plan. It has said that it is going to limit the growth of funding to three provinces: Alberta, B.C. and Ontario.
I think that the Speaker and the House should be aware that this involves just under 50 per cent of the people who are in need of assistance and 50 per cent of the children who are in need of protection in this country. The government is suddenly breaking up the partnership, which affects a large percentage of those who have been assisted by the Canada Assistance Plan.
The government has indicated that the cuts may be as low as $75 million to $80 million a year. The provinces of course have calculated that the significance is going to be dramatically higher, in the area of $400 and some million this year and $600 million next year.
Part of this increase is caused by the dramatic increase in unemployment, which of course is caused by the fiscal monetary policy of the government. But the provinces are being told that they have to pick up the consequences of higher income assistance case loads and more people becoming dependent because of unemployment, and that the federal government is not going to be involved in the cost of that. It is going to dump it on the provinces; it is going to break up the partnership.
A week ago the Minister of National Health and Welfare, with great fanfare, announced his family violence program or initiative against family violence: $136 million spread over five years. There is $23.6 million this year, out of which the minister himself said only $15 million was new money. At the same time, the cost to the provinces is going to be $400 million.
What does the Canada Assistance Plan fund? It funds investigation of child abuse. It funds counselling of family problems. It funds the operation of shelters,

March 4, 1991
The Budget
including shelters for battered women. It funds the treatment of children who have been sexually abused. It funds alternate care for children.
On the one hand, with great fanfare, the minister announced a program with $15 million or $22 million in a year and at the same time takes away from the provinces $400 million that is designed to do that very thing. No wonder the provinces are beginning to ask: Where is the partnership? Where is the trust that is normally involved in a partnership?
It simply is not good enough for the government to try flimflam financing, to try this shuffle the peas concept of moving money around and announcing that it is starting new programs when in fact the very core or heart of the ability of the provinces to finance the services that would go a long way in dealing with family violence has been reduced.
The other area of this budget that impacts very much upon families is the reduction in social housing. There is another 15 per cent reduction per year in the commitment toward new social housing; $86 million for all of Canada for a year. My own riding could easily take the whole budget for social housing in Canada and still have a backlog and still have a need.
There seems to be a deliberate, two-pronged attack in this budget. One is the erosion of all social programs: social housing, medicare, and the Canada Assistance Plan. It is the type of erosion people talked about during the free trade debate, that one of the goals of this government was to Americanize our social security and health care systems, to Balkanize it, to fractionalize it, to privatize it, and to make it equal to the United States.
Most of us know that it would be disastrous for working Canadians and Canadians with limited income if the government were able to achieve its goal of harmonization with the United States.
The other goal of this government, as seen in this budget, seems simply to be to dump the problem on to the provinces. It seems simply to say: "We do not understand fair taxation. We do not understand how we can bring in and maintain our social programs. If only we had a proper monetary policy so that high interest rates were not driving up the deficit. We do not understand how we can have fair taxation for profitable corporations
to pay at least a minimal tax. What we will do, because we do not understand or have no will, is we will simply dump the problem on to the provinces and let the provinces try to figure out how they are going to deal with the financial consequences".
In my own municipality of Surrey I know how the province is going to deal with it. Unfortunately, it is simply going to say that the necessary additional beds for Surrey Memorial Hospital are not there. They can no longer afford to finance them. They will not worry about the fact that we only have 1.1 acute care beds per 1,000 population, compared to the average of 3.3 beds across the province or the goal set by most organizations and medical people of about 3.4 acute care beds per 1,000 population. They will simply not be in a position to finance any additional medical facilities. They will simply dump the problem further down on the community. It is the same with post-secondary education. The cutbacks mean that the provinces are going to have less money, which simply means that they are going to say to a municipality like mine that we cannot expand Kwantlen College, that we cannot worry about the fact that there were thousands of students turned away this year; that they simply do not have the money.
In summation, this budget, particularly in the area of social services and health care, means that the federal government has abandoned its partnership with the provinces in providing services to the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who was just speaking was making some comments throughout his speech about health care. I note with interest lately that the newly elected premier of Ontario has realized that it is a lot harder to produce than it is to talk. Comments are already being made about the benefits of health care, that maybe there should be a type of clawback tax put in place for those who benefit from health care services in our country.
I just wonder if the member would care to comment on that. Is this his view, that a Canadian who receives the benefit of our medical services and health care services should be taxed as a taxable benefit and therefore have a clawback type tax in place? Is that the member's view?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the premier of Ontario is beginning to realize the financial shambles that the previous Liberal government left them in. He
March 4, 1991

was told during the election that there was a $23 million surplus, and now he finds out there is a three-quarter of a billion dollar deficit. And, yes, he is having to make some hard choices.
As far as comments that there should be a clawback are concerned, the only people I have ever heard talking about a clawback are the Tories and the Liberals. Certainly the New Democratic Party has always stood against any type of fee for service, any type of two-tiered health care system, anything that prevents accessibility to our health care system.
It has been proven time and time again that if those kinds of systems are brought in, the only people who are hurt are the poor. It does nothing at all to assist in the curtailment of costs. It does nothing to rationalize properly our health care system or services. Therefore, I would certainly reject any type of clawback system in terms of health care.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my colleague to comment on the Canadian unity aspects of this budget.
To me it is a great tragedy that this budget is a strong blow to Canadian unity, at the very time when we should be building our pride in being Canadian. It seems to me universal medicare and our social programs and our post-secondary education programs are being undermined. When we ask Canadians what makes them proud to be a Canadian, those are the very things they will mention first. This government in this budget is undermining them.
I would like to ask my colleague if he would comment again on the consequences of the federal government withdrawing financing and, in effect, withdrawing any kind of national power in the development and the ensuring of universal medicare and social programs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think there is a great threat to unity in this budget. The Conservatives feel that the whole question of how you build a nation is simply a matter of dealing and tinkering with constitutional problems. Most citizens in this country are much more concerned about the unifying forces that they understand as their rights and obligations within the country.
The Budget
They are very proud of medicare. They feel it is one of the things that has held this country together, that we do have a national program, that we do have national standards, and that Canadians do not fear illness in the same way that Americans do. Americans always fear they will become totally bankrupt if they get a major illness and are under insured. Even the ones who carry insurance find that a year later they will not be reinsured in the United States.
One of the more interesting programs which I think people should watch is a documentary which Walter Cronkite did, comparing the American and Canadian health care systems, because it showed that we do have problems. Those problems are mainly not enough financing to keep up with the increase in technology. However, it did show in terms of the well-being of Canadians and their ability to cope and deal with health problems, we were far ahead.
There are many things in this budget that I am concerned about not only from the program point of view, but also their impact on unity. This is a step towards this term that my finance minister in B.C. Mr. Couvelier likes to talk about, disentanglement. What it means is that the federal government is starting to, without even negotiating, throw up their hands and say to the provinces, "We are going to get out of certain areas. We are not going to be partners in certain areas. We are not going to even wait for a constitutional conference or constitutional change. We are simply going to abandon medicare. We are simply going to abandon our obligation to social programs".
In the fundamental sense, that is probably going to have more impact on the unity in this country than any other significant matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a brief comment and ask the member who made, I think, some very important and reasonable comments about how this budget is going to help destroy medicare in Canada.
He had just started touching on the question I would like to put to him when he made reference to the finance minister in British Columbia, our home province and the current premier of B.C., who I believe the member has had some experience with in local governments when

March 4, 1991
The Budget
Mr. Vander Zalm was a Liberal. My constituents are asking me questions and perhaps there is some good political advice I can get from the member.
Mr. Vander Zalm in B.C. on the one hand talks about how the federal government has to pull back out of health care, perhaps do away with the fledgling forestry department and cut federal spending. Yet at the same time, when the federal government does cut funding to the province of British Columbia, he is taking the federal government to court, challenging the actions of the federal government.
The question I would like to put to the member is this. What kind of political approach is this from the premier of British Columbia? Is there some kind of consistent argument we might be able to see in what Mr. Vander Zalm is saying or is it a case really where Social Credit, Conservatives and Liberals are really talking about of the same thing, and that is the destruction of much of what we have come to know as Canada?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have a tendency to try to forget my experience with the premier when he was the Liberal mayor of Surrey and I was an alderman on Surrey Council. At that time he was very erratic. I guess over the years he has continued to be very erratic.
Certainly I do not really look at his statements where one day he says that the federal government should get out of medicare. The next day when the federal government starts to withdraw he says: "No, that's wrong". That type of erratic behaviour certainly does not show any consistent leadership.
I guess I am not surprised after being involved with him for 20 years, and knowing his style and his erratic approach to politics and social problems and issues that that is true. However, I am more concerned about the inconsistencies we see evolving in Canada from the government in terms of policy.
At one time the sharing of costs was 50-50. The provinces paid 50; the federal government paid 50. Now the provinces are paying 63 per cent of health care costs and the federal government 37 per cent. With the budget that was brought in last week, I am sure this figure will go down to much more like 65-35. That, of course, is the end of any equal partnership.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would really like to bring this debate back to a sense of reality
rather than the sense of mythology that has been built up by my colleagues opposite from over the mountains.
In that vein I am pleased to speak on the budget presented in this House last week by the Hon. Michael Wilson, Minister of Finance. This is an important blueprint for the economic health of Canada, both over the next year and in years subsequent.
The people of Macleod have told me that they want fiscal responsibility from the federal government. We want a bright financial future for our children, not one that has been mortgaged away. Whether I am in Vulcan, Red Deer Lake, or in the Crow's Nest Pass, the message remains the same: "Let's get Canada's financial house in order".
This budget sets out an achievable plan which will meet these concerns I so often hear from fellow Albertans in southern Alberta. It puts in legislation for the first time-this is a historic moment-the requirement for government to restrain spending. It is a major milestone.
When I was first elected to this House in 1988 I brought an important message from the people of Macleod: Restrain government spending and get the deficit under control.
Thoughtful southern Albertans tell me above anything else, their biggest concern is Canada's deficit. They realize that our country has been living well beyond its means and governments have to be ready to say: "Enough is enough".
The finance minister has made it abundantly clear: "Enough is enough".
Our national debt will soon reach $400 billion. That is $15,000 for every man, woman, and child. Interest on this debt is now the single largest expense faced by the government. Interest on the debt alone will cost more than $43 billion next year. That is more money than is spent on old age security, on unemployment insurance, and family allowances combined. It will take tough, determined action to solve Canada's fundamental economic and fiscal problems.
Our government has declared all-out war on the deficit. We have listened to Canadians who have told us to use the GST as a tool to fight the deficit and just as in Alberta we used the Alberta Heritage Savings and Trust Fund for surplus funds, now at the federal level we have
March 4, 1991

created and are using the Debt Servicing and Reduction Fund to manage the debt.
I must give credit to my colleagues from Lethbridge, from the neighbouring riding to mine, because he has been working away on this, I know, ever since I have been in the House and I know he worked on it before. As an important means to ensure that next time there is an election, and the time there is an election after that, that spending does not become the way to go, that restraint continues to remain an important objective of this government. I give my colleague from Lethbridge full credit for determinedly pursued this question. I know other members worked with him as well.
All GST revenues will be used to bring the public debt under control. Also flowing into that fund will be revenues from the sale of Crown corporations and contributions by individuals and organizations.
The people of Macleod have made it loud and clear that they do not want the GST to be a cash cow to be milked by any government. They do not want revenues from the new tax, the replacement tax, to be used for new and expensive programs. I have been told countless times by constituents at public meetings, coffee shops and on the street that the GST should be used to fight the deficit. It is good advice, and the government has heeded that advice.
With the creation of the Debt Servicing and Reduction Fund, Canadians are now reassured that GST revenues will not be used for new program creation. Legislation will be introduced with that very goal in mind. Of course, as is the case with all government accounts, this fund will be reviewed annually by the Auditor General. Revenues going into the fund will be applied first against the cost of servicing the debt, that is, the interest, and as revenues grow over time, as the economy grows, these revenues will be used to reduce outstanding debt. This is further evidence of the commitment to fight the deficit and the national debt.
To ensure that this spending track is met, the government will legislate expenditure limits on annual program spending for the next five years. Of course, some flexibility will be provided to meet a very limited set of contingencies. This will change significantly the way
The Budget
government manages its expenditures. While new programs to meet new needs will be possible, they will have to be funded from the total legislated spending ceiling.
This government is the first in Canada's history to legislate a ceiling on its spending. It is an historic development and a critical step which helps the House of Commons and the elected government place restraint upon and give political direction to the bureaucracies and the bureaucrats that serve the government and the people of Canada. Of course, this will be of interest to students of public policy because I believe it is a good policy.
But the achievement is also critical to those who serve as elected representatives of Canada. The people have been calling for restraint and through these measures the government of Canada, the House of Commons, is meeting those demands. Much of the nation is now facing recession and this government is going to ensure that the will of the people of Canada is reflected in the federal system. That is only appropriate and it is only fair to all Canadians.
Canadians have told us to control federal spending. We have responded. Legislation will limit growth and total federal program spending to just 3 per cent per year after 1991-92. This is proof positive of the government's commitment in its fight against the deficit.
If you were to talk to people on the street in Longview or Fort Macleod or other communities in southern Alberta within my riding, you would quickly realize that fiscal restraint is what they want. Incidentally, I might note the hon. member for Kamloops sent me a note recently, as he did to all western members, encouraging them to vote against this budget, create an election. This is the most outrageous thing I have ever heard. Well, the hon. member should grow up. He was bom, in all places, in High River, Alberta. He grew up in Longview, Alberta. Both communities are in my riding, and let me tell you, the folks back home do not want an election. The folks back home do not want us to vote against this budget. They are saying get on with the business of government; get on with the business of restraining expenditures. I do not know where the member from Kamloops has been for those many years since he left Longview, Alberta, but he has wandered a long way.

March 4, 1991
The Budget
Macleod residents do not want to be bought with their own money. Nothing offends them more. They do not want to see lavish government expenditures at the expense of their children. Legislated spending controls provide all Canadians a guarantee of restraint.
Now, if we are to succeed in reducing the deficit, we must practise sustained spending restraint. The government took further action in this budget to restrain program spending and spending on government operations to ensure further reduction of the deficit. The Expenditure Control Plan was announced in 1990 and has now been extended for three years.
This plan affects a wide variety of government spending, but it makes some important exemptions. Those exemptions include: income support programs for seniors, families and veterans; unemployment insurance; equalization; Canada Assistance Plan payments to lower income provinces; and Indian and Inuit programs.
These are all important programs where, quite clearly, this government is demonstrating its commitment to social programs in this country. In fact, the best social program we can provide is a strong economy, employment for Canadians, and the opportunity for Canadians to build their own future. It is through these strong measures that we provide a guarantee of a strong future for all Canadians.
The Expenditure Control Plan will restrain spending growth in a number of areas after 1991-92. For example, these include Canada Assistance Plan payments to the fiscally stronger provinces, funding for science and technology and official development assistance. Other areas of spending will be frozen, such as per capita transfers to the provinces under the Established Program Financing. Even so, total transfers continue to grow with provincial populations.
In all, programs exempt from the extension of the Expenditure Control Plan account for about 60 per cent of program spending and will grow at an annual average rate of 3.9 per cent from 1991-92 to 1995-96. All other spending will grow at an average annual rate of 1.7 per cent. These are tremendous commitments to the need for restraint.
The cost of government operations has been closely controlled since 1984. In real dollar figures, they have actually declined. We intensified this effort in December
1989 with the announcement of several new cost cutting measures.
Canadians want the burden of restraint to fall equally on everyone. My constituents often tell me that they are willing to do their part, but elected officials, civil servants and others in the public sector must be willing to do their share as well. The restraint and efficiency measures introduced to government management are proof that the government has again listened.
The Prime Minister and his cabinet will have their ministerial salaries frozen for one year. Salaries of senators and members of Parliament which currently increase at the rate of inflation minus 1 per cent will be limited to the lesser of that or the average public service settlements.
My constituents want the burden of a weaker economy shared by the civil service. Public servants have not felt the pain of this recession in the same way as do private sector employees. While many people have lost jobs in the private sector, there have been no recent job losses in the public sector, and this is an important question of fairness to all Canadians.
I agree strongly with the government's position not to contemplate civil service wage increases of over 3 per cent a year for the next three years.
I also support the salary limitations placed on executive level bureaucrats and the intention to reduce the number of senior level officials. All Canadians must share the strengths and weaknesses of our economic performance.
These measures will protect jobs, maintain service levels and aid and fight against the deficit. Over the next five years, the government will realize savings of $3.6 billion through these measures.
The government has looked at other areas to reduce its spending as well. I strongly support the government's reconsideration of several large expenditure decisions. The government has looked at a number of questions and has decided it is time to put some of these issues on the back burner and consider them down the road.
I saw newspaper reports earlier last week quoting members opposite, asking the government to increase spending substantially and to ignore the deficit. For example, the member for Essex-Windsor urged the

Minister of Finance to "abandon old Tory deficit cutting policies".
The member for Windsor West said: "The priority at this point has to shift to dealing with the recession." The story goes on to say that "Mr. Gray would not specify how much of an increase in the deficit he would be willing to see".
The last time we were in a recession, the Liberal government of the day ignored the deficit. The deficit doubled from $14 billion to $28 billion per year during that period. That is truly offensive. We cannot afford to do that now. We are still paying the price of those misguided policies of the early 1980s.
The opposition seems to believe that spending more money will make the world's problems go away. It did not work in the past and it is not going to work now. Canadians are telling all politicians that they cannot continue spending that they do not have. Canadians are right.
The people of Macleod have stated clearly that they want the deficit tackled. Our deficit targets are right in line. Despite recessionary pressures, despite the tremendous difficulties of keeping the deficit to where it is now, down to $30.5 billion, there were tremendous pressures to increase that deficit. I commend the Minister of Finance for his tremendous achievement in keeping it at that level.
In 1992-93, with recovery and with lower interest rates, the deficit will fall below $25 billion for the first time in a decade. The need for new federal borrowing in financial markets, the need for us to go out and ask to borrow money from others in other parts of the world or from other Canadians, will be eliminated in 1993-94. That will be a great day for Canada.
The deficit is the government's number one priority, but we have to remain mindful, and we do remain mindful, of the current recession. The government has allocated extra money to where it is needed most. Program spending will increase by $7.5 billion in the next fiscal year.
The majority of this increase will go to three areas: $3 billion will go to the assistance of the unemployed, an important contribution in that area; $1.6 billion will go to the elderly; and $1.3 billion for farmers who face tough times.
The Budget
This budget allocation for agriculture is critically important in my riding of Macleod as it is based primarily on agriculture, much of the riding. The $1.3 billion commitment in the budget is the government's recognition, yet again. We have done this year after year after year under this government, the recognition of the importance of agriculture in the Canadian economy and the social fabric of so much of rural and small-town Canada. It is good news for agriculture, it is good news for the small communities that depend on agriculture and so it is good news for the whole riding of Macleod.
Farm leaders across Canada were quick to offer their praise for the budget. Alex Graham, chairman of the Prairie Wheat Pools said; "It's a real positive sign of government's commitment to agriculture". Don Knoerr, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture said: "You obviously have to be pleased that the need of farmers, though desperate, has been recognized by the federal government". Harvey McEwen, president of the Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association said: "It's an extremely good sign. The funding has bought us time to dig ourselves out of this."
There can be no doubt of the importance agriculture plays in Canada's economy. The government has recognized this in this budget and it is supported by the agricultural community. I might add that it is something that is critically important across western Canada.
As a member of Parliament from western Canada, I am heartened once again by the commitment shown and the leadership shown by the Minister of Agriculture, and to the commitment of this government to follow through, to support our farmers in the midst of this, particularly, the international trade war between the Americans and the Europeans. This has been a problem for all grain producing countries for years and we are all optimistic that through the negotiations at GATT over the next year or two that we actually will get to a point to deal with some of these issues in the international context.
In the meantime, this government stands by agriculture.
In conclusion, the 1991-92 federal budget, I think, can be best described as tough but fair. The government has confronted the deficit head on, but all Canadians will share the burden. The budget is a financial blueprint to brighter economic times and a more secure future for

March 4, 1991
The Budget
our children and grandchildren. More important, it is what Canadians want.
As I said earlier, the people of Macleod sent a message with me when I was elected in 1988. One of those messages was to restrain government spending and get the deficit under control. This budget reflects what my constituents have requested.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question as well as a comment on some of the figures that were quoted by the hon. member for Macleod. He talked about the extra spending by the government, and I believe he mentioned a figure of $3 billion for unemployment insurance payments.
I want to make it clear to those who are listening to that statement. It sounds as if this is coming directly on behalf of the largesse of the government. It is not quite that simple. The government, as the hon. member knows-and I see him smiling over there-is not lashing out with $3 billion to the unemployment insurance fund. Indeed, I am sure the hon. member will recall, as will other members in the House, that Bill C-21 effectively took the government out of the unemployment insurance business. It was my understanding that, previous to this, the government paid about 25 per cent-in fact, I think it was 26 per cent-of all of the unemployment insurance money. In the days when the unemployment insurance fund was worth around $13 billion, the government contributed around $3 billion.
That $3 billion that it used to contribute is not the $3 billion that it is contributing that is referred to by the hon. member. Indeed, I do believe that there has been some recanting on the part of the government, or change of heart, if you like, in how that money has been collected.
The Minister of Finance in his budget speech last week said that there were no new tax increases. A tax increase comes in many forms-and I do not want to talk about the cigarette tax. But an area that really appalled me and indeed has a lot of my constituents, and I am sure Canadians all across the country, in a bit of an uproar is the bizarre increase in unemployment insurance premiums, to the tune of 24 per cent, on both the part of the employee and the employer. Taken in itself, I think that
is pretty terrible. But when you add it to the percentage increase that had occurred as a result of Bill C-21, raising the unemployment insurance premiums for the individual essentially 50 per cent in about a year and a half and the same for the employers, then we have a number of things happening. We have the employees paying tax money so that they can get it back in the form of unemployment insurance; and the employers have to pay more. So, what we have is a tax increase for the individual employees, who in many cases cannot afford another cent from their pay cheques; and indeed the businesses, many of which are small businesses, have to fork over more payments as well.
This, I can assure the hon. member, may be given by the government, but it is given by the government because it is received from the government by those people who are paying the extra unemployment insurance premiums to make up in the next year or two, depending on how you count it and depending on how many we have employed, between $2 billion and $3 billion. So, that equation is about right.
I would like the hon. member, in all fairness, to clarify that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank my hon. colleague opposite for his very thoughtful intervention. But he knows as well as any other member in this House that what the government has asked for is an additional $2.70 a week. He knows as well as any other member in the House that what is required in this country is an unemployment insurance program that is going to be fully funded, that is going to be able to provide the benefits to Canadians who are unemployed. He knows that the people who are going to be able to pay for this are the Canadians who are employed, and that it is only fair that that should be the case.
I think he recognizes that the goal here is to provide for real unemployment insurance. "Insurance" is the name of the program. The burden falls fairly on Canadians who are employed, and the benefits fall fairly to those Canadians who are temporarily unemployed before they get back into the market. I think the hon. member would like to paint this from a certain perspective and that is his prerogative as a member of the House. I see him smiling. We all recognize that that is what he is trying to do.
March 4, 1991

Realistically, you have to deal with questions like this in a real world. Who is going to pay for additional money if it is just going to be going into the deficit? It is going to be the hon. member's children, my children and the children of our constituents today. You cannot continue to force the deficit off into the future where somebody down the road is going to pay. You have got to start dealing with the question now and here today.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very illuminating to hear a speech from the hon. member in which he talks about the hardships, that the deficit is causing the need for cutbacks. We are ready to slash those civil servants down in Ottawa. The fact that there is the same number as there were back in 1974 is not mentioned. But when it comes to $1.3 billion for agriculture, that is okay. That is really important that we get money to those farmers.
We do not worry about spending money on job creation. After all, our children and grandchildren are going to have to pay for that because it is going to be added to the deficit. It is okay if 1.5 million Canadians are out of work. It is okay if we lose 288,000 jobs in the manufacturing sector, half of them permanently. But send that $1.3 billion out to Macleod, Alberta, because that is where we need it.
I would like to ask the hon. member what he thinks of this. This is what the present Minister of Finance had to say about governments devoting money to job creation during the last recession when the government at that time put $500 million into job creation. This is what he said, and I quote: "The minister announced a $500 million job creation program. I guess we have to say, Mr. Speaker, it is a step in the right direction. They have addressed the problem of unemployment in this budget, but it is a very small step. Does the hon. member agree with the present Minister of Finance when he expressed the view in 1982 that governments should devote resources to job creation, or does he agree with the Minister of Finance today who says: "Let the unemployed just sit out there and stew without jobs"?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year when I had the opportunity to address this House on the subject of the federal budget, I compared the Minister of Finance to the emperor who had no clothes. I said that, lurking in the budget document of one year ago, could be found a tacit admission of failure on the part of the minister.
While he was not prepared to admit until the month of October that Canada was enduring a recession, it seemed plain enough to me at the time, that the minister's empty rhetoric signalled a recession under way or about to begin, as well as the realization that past policies had not worked.
Well, the made-in-Canada recession of 1990-91 is now beginning its twelfth month. Almost 1.5 million Canadians are unemployed and unlike last year when it was necessary for the minister's deception to be pointed out, this year it is plain for all to see that this is a minister and a government that have no ideas, no vision for the future, no compassion for the unemployed and homeless and nothing to offer the people of Canada at this time.
Many Canadians now feel that they do not have much to which they can look forward and, regrettably, with the presentation of the 1991 budget, the Conservative government has, if anything, contributed to the despair and discontent that plagues Canada at this time.

So we have to add this to the tragic list of a record 5,991 bankruptcies recorded in January. The Tory government has no vision for the future. Theirs is a vision that will bankrupt the country. This Budget smells of despair.

In his own presentation to Parliament, the finance minister has as much as admitted that the economic crisis he brought on is now beyond his control. While the minister says that this budget is designed to give Canadians confidence, that it provides leadership and direction, his own projections quickly make it impossible to share the optimism inherent in the rhetoric. His so-called road to recovery is absolutely meaningless for the
1.5	million Canadians whom he says will stay unemployed for 1991 and 1992.
His recent conversion to concern about high interest rates provides no prospect for relief for mortgage holders and small businesses that will still be confronted, according to the minister, with interest rates around 10 per cent and real rates of about 7 per cent. These projections indicate that the Canadian dollar will remain high and, therefore, Canadian exports will continue to be at a competitive disadvantage.
Furthermore, the government treats the deficit problem in this country as strictly a numbers game with no apparent appreciation for the need to invest in people.

Once again, the Tories prove they don't know what they are doing. The 1991 Budget shows they are as lost as they have been for the past seven years.

In the final analysis, they have allowed Canada to drift into engagement in fierce competition in an unforgiving global economy without being equipped to meet the challenge.
Worse still, much of the current economic hardship faced by Canadians was deliberately planned by the government. In the Prime Minister's own words: "We have induced an economic slowdown".
March 4, 1991

subsubtopic: HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the shelters for the homeless across Canada are full and overflowing. The best estimate of the number of homeless is vague; somewhere between 130,000 and 250,000 people.
The recent budget has sent another crippling blow to these homeless Canadians. The government has drastically reduced the effectiveness of the federal housing program by cutting new housing initiatives.
According to the Canadian Housing Renewal Association, the 15 per cent cut will result in the loss of more than 3,000 desperately needed housing units. By extending those cuts into 1995-96, we will have lost more than $400 million from the housing budget and thousands of homes for Canadians.
When will the government recognize the problem of the homeless in this country? When will the government devote the necessary time and resources, first, to find out exactly how many Canadians are homeless and, second, take a leadership role in co-ordinating the efforts of all levels of government and the private sector to ensure that adequate housing is available to all Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, although they lost the Canada Games flag by one point, Quebec athletes behaved like winners at the closing ceremonies in Charlottetown yesterday. They were the first to rise to give Ontario a standing ovation when it was awarded the games flag.
Claude Hardy, who headed Quebec's delegation, said that to win the flag, they had to stay up there, and that is what they did.
Quebec athletes won 150 medals, including 63 gold, and set two new games records. Quebec finished one point behind Ontario, losing 256.5 to 257.5.
Three cheers for our Quebec athletes!

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, year after year the fishing fleets of the European community have taken more fish than they agreed to take. The word for this is theft. The Europeans are stealing from the fishing families and communities throughout Atlantic Canada. While this federal government imposes severe cuts on Canadian fishermen, it has proven itself incapable of stopping the Europeans from overfishing year in and year out.
In 1990, the Europeans took five times more fish than they agreed to take in the area beyond Canada's 200-mile limit.
From Dr. Les Harris in his report on northern cod, the Fisheries Council of Canada, fishing communities and provincial governments the call has been the same: stop foreign overfishing and extend jurisdiction.
It is time to put the Europeans on notice. It is either stop overfishing or next year find themselves fishing inside newly claimed Canadian waters.
It is time for this federal government to start protecting the interests and futures of Canadian fishing families and communities.

subtopic: THE LATE HELEN HUNLEY LIEUTENANT-GOVERNOR OF ALBERTA
THE LATE HELEN HUNLEY LIEUTENANT-GOVERNOR OF ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the final week in the term of the 12th Lieutenant-Governor of the Province of Alberta. As an Albertan and as a friend of Her Honour, it is appropriate to pay tribute to Her Honour Helen Hunley.
Ms. Hunley has had an outstanding career, serving first as a lieutenant in the Canadian Women's Army Corps in World War II, a successful business person, a counsellor and mayor of Rocky Mountain House, and later a member of the Legislative Assembly of Alberta.

March 4, 1991
She served in our provincial cabinet as Solicitor General and Minister of Social Services and Community Health. She retired from active politics in 1979 but was prevailed upon to accept the position of Lieutenant-Governor of Alberta in 1985.
Her Honour tackled this position as she has everything else in her life, by committing herself completely to the role. She has done absolutely everything that could be expected of a Lieutenant-Governor and has done it well. She has fulfilled her vice-regal duties with dignity and dedication and has earned the respect and admiration of all Albertans.

Mr. Speaker, on humanitarian grounds, I call upon the Minister of Employment and Immigration to issue Arthur and Helena Gras and their two children a permit to remain in Canada.
Mr. Gras, a Polish sailor, and his family are now under threat of deportation after being in Canada seeking refugee status for three years.
Humanitarian grounds are based on the fact that both children are Canadian citizens. One child suffers from a rare medical condition that doctors have verified cannot be adequately treated in Poland. Mr. Gras, if he had not been caught in the refugee backlog, would have been deemed a political refugee when he first arrived in Canada in 1988. Mr. Gras has been able to secure employment and the family has adjusted well to Canada.
I ask the minister to show compassion and common sense and stop the deportation of the Gras family.

Mr. Speaker, in June 1989 the world watched in horror as the Chinese government brutally crushed a pro-democracy movement in Tiananmen Square.
That same government has now quietly stepped up its trials and sentencing of participants of the pro-democracy movement, perhaps because the world's attention continues to be focused on the situation in the Persian Gulf.
There is almost total secrecy surrounding the trials in China. Observers from Canada and other western nations have been thwarted in their efforts to monitor this further oppression by the Chinese government.
The war in the gulf is over and, as we work for a new world order, let us not forget there are hundreds, perhaps thousand, of young people in China behind bars and facing an uncertain future, all because they wanted their government to move more quickly toward democratic reform.
We in Canada can and must stand up for the principle of free expression and oppose the use of force against unarmed demonstrators. The Chinese government must be made aware, in no uncertain terms, that Canada is watching.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the success of the United Nations military action against Iraq will act as a precedent and deterrent to other bullies who attack legitimate nations.
However, there is another benefit less obvious. It will no longer be necessary for countries to spend billions and billions of dollars for weapons to protect themselves from others. In short, they can now choose to spend money on economic development and social programs and rely on the United Nations to defend their legitimate borders.
I am sure you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that this is a legitimate concept for Canada to promote at the United Nations and elsewhere.

Mr. Speaker, Keith Spicer's statement that Canadians could not care less how the Spicer Commission is administered is outrageous, at a time when the government is making Canadian taxpayers pay for its own administrative incompetence.
Taxpayers do care how the Spicer Commission is administered.


Taxpayers do care about the $25 million they will have to pay for a so-called commission that has lost all credibility.
Quebecers do care about Robert Normand's statements that the Spicer Commission has trivialized Quebec issues.
Mr. Spicer has shown poor judgment and a lack of openness, both to an unacceptable degree.
You are right!
He should resign immediately, and the government should suspend the proceedings of this commission and order an inquiry to clear up what we could already call the Spicer Commission scandal.

Mr. Speaker, during the conflict in the Persian Gulf, troops from our Canadian Forces played a major role. Canada did its fair share with all coalition countries in supporting the UN Security Council's resolutions.
During the conflict, many other members of our Forces worked long hours here in Canada to co-ordinate our activities in the Middle East.

I am sure all members of Parliament will agree with my request to have the Minister of National Defence strike a commemorative medal for our members of the Armed Forces. Such a medal would show the appreciation of all Canadians for these dedicated men and women.

Now is the time to show how proud we are of our troops, and I think a medal would be appropriate.

Mr. Speaker, this government purports to cut the deficit by saving money, by cutbacks in health, education and the environment.
As a Scots Canadian, we learned a long time ago that you can save money on little things and then you build it up so it becomes a big thing.
I want to suggest to the government that it can save waste in government in little things. I am not just talking about the Minister of Communications' trips and institutions, although it could save on those.
Let us take a look at the official residences: $500,000 was spent on housing in the last six months for the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition. For the Leader of the Opposition, $27,000 was spent on furniture so he could move in; $17,600 to paint the place. That is a little bit more than they pay in Beausejour. For linens, $11,000, and at 24 Sussex Drive, $629 was spent for slush matting and $1,080 for pest control.
Who is that? The Bloc Quebecois? I don't know.
My Scottish grandmother once said that if you really want to save money, you add up all the little expenditures and you get a big cut in expenditures. The government should cut this wasteful expenditure in Stornoway and 24 Sussex Drive.

Mr. Speaker, the recent federal budget is right for the times.
Indeed, as the Treasury Board minister said, the present cost and complexity of government operations can no longer be justified to Canadians. Accordingly, this government will legislate mandatory program spending limits. These should have been in place 20 years ago, but it is not too late.
For the first time there will be in place a law putting ceilings on the amount that politicians can spend. Canadians concerned about GST revenues being used to fund new programs will applaud the establishment of the debt servicing and reduction fund, guaranteeing that those revenues will be solely dedicated to deficit reduction.
The Public Service wage cap, reductions in the layers of bureaucratic management, the 10 per cent cut in senior management, and cuts in grants and contributions send welcome signals to Canadians who are sick and tired of the costs of big government.
This government provides the reductions and reforms that are absolutely necessary if government is to have the funds necessary for essential safety net programs and services. It provides the impetus for lower interest rates

Mr. Speaker, Canadians rejoiced with the announcement of the ceasefire in the gulf and the removal of Saddam Hussein's army from Kuwait.
Now that the hostilities have ended, we can focus our attention on rebuilding a safe and secure environment for all the peoples of the world, including the Middle East. Canada has shown leadership in proposing a world summit, under the auspices of the United Nations, on the control of instruments of war and weapons of mass destruction. The agenda should include conventional arms, chemical weapons, missile systems, nuclear and biological weapons.
I wish to commend the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the initiatives they have taken today in proposing a world summit on arms control. This is paramount in establishing a new world order for lasting peace.
This is the time to deal with arms control. This is the time to strengthen the United Nations.

Mr. Speaker, whose words are these: "Governments must conduct themselves like private citizens. Borrow, if necessary, for capital assets such as a new home, but pay as you go for current expenditures, like the groceries"?
He went on to say:
The leaders of the 60s and 70s have placed a first mortgage on the future of Canada. The leaders of the 80s and 90s are placing a second mortgage on the same asset. There is no equity left. We must once and for all put an end to the suffocating debt-load we are placing on the backs of our children.
Who spoke those words? The Minister of Finance? The Prime Minister? No, Mr. Speaker, it was the premier of the province of New Brunswick, Frank McKenna. It sounds as if he agrees with us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question should bear a consumer warning: "Caution: Listening to these statements may be hazardous to the truth".
Nothing could be further from the truth than the suggestion that the federal government wants to destroy medicare. One thing that is clear, however, is that Canadians are spending some $2,000 per citizen, per year on health care. Looked at in terms of percentage of gross domestic product, only the United States among the western industrialized countries spends a higher percentage of GDP than Canada does on health care.
The real challenge for us in protecting medicare for the future is not simply to continue to inflate the system, but rather to ask ourselves whether the dollars that we are spending are as wisely spent as could be the case.

Oral Questions
For example, I would have hoped that the hon. member would have strongly endorsed the position that was taken by the Minister of Finance, which will reduce by probably 100,000 the number of young Canadians who are smoking and, along the way, save literally thousands of lives and tens of millions of taxpayers' dollars on medicare.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has characterized as being untruthful a direct quote by the Minister of Finance which many of us heard on CBC radio this morning. I will leave it to the Minister of Finance to settle with the Minister of National Health and Welfare on this, but this is an exact quote.
The Minister of Finance laid out the blueprint for the phasing out of federal transfer payments for health care in his own budget document last week. The National Council of Welfare, the government-created advisory body to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, has said, speaking about these cutbacks: "Without federal leverage, provinces could impose user fees-a backward step that would deter poor people in particular from seeking the care they need".
Why does the minister and his government want the provinces to take this kind of backward step?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not challenge what was said by the Minister of Finance. I challenged what was said by the hon. member for Windsor West when he suggested that the federal government's goal was to destroy medicare by the back door, a view I might mention that is not shared by Madam Begin, the former Liberal Minister of National Health and Welfare. In an article on Saturday in The Globe and Mail: "Medicare will survive," Begin says. "Former health minister says federal cuts not threat to system".
Once again we have the members of the Liberal Party being confused about the total amount of transfers being made between Ottawa and the provinces. At the very same time as they are complaining about reductions in the amount of cash being transferred, they ignore the fact that tax points, which have exactly the same net effect to the federal treasury and to the provincial treasury, are increasing and that the growth in transfers
from the federal government to the provinces will be more than 1 per cent for EPF this year.
If hon. members wish to protect medicare, it is important we put the federal government's finances in place so that we can ensure the stability of Canada's social programs for the future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Today, leading indicators continued to drop dramatically. The recession continues. However, according to the Budget, all is well, as the government says on page 52: "-consumption is projected to rebound vigorously in the second half of the year-".
How can the government expect consumption to get us out of this recession, when the Budget projects that one out of ten Canadians will be unemployed, and when the government is attacking people's salaries and the GST is taking billions of dollars out of the pockets of people across this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the indicator to which the hon. member referred does not give us any new information. I think everyone in this House was quite aware of the situation we had in December.
I agree it is a difficult situation, and that is why it is so important for us to take steps to get out of this situation. In this respect, I would say that the latest Budget brought down by my colleague, the Minister of Finance-who would have liked to be in the House but was held up by the storm, on the highway between Montreal and Ottawa-creates exactly those conditions the economy will need to recover.
Of course we must act, but we must deal with the real causes of the problem and create an economic climate that will allow interest rates to go down and be conducive to economic recovery and thus increased employment.

Mr. Speaker, I say to this government; let's get real. The leading

indicators continue to drop sharply right across this country. This means more people without jobs; it means more children without enough food; it means more families struggling just to make ends meet.
On Saturday the Minister of Finance said he had made mistakes in past budgets. Will this government admit that this budget this past week was a mistake? Will it help the jobless instead of hurting the jobless? Will it cut the big gap between interest rates in the United States and interest rates in Canada? In short, will it do something about this recession instead of trying to make this recession worse for people?

speechtext: If the hon. gentleman were to look at his desk he would see a dark piece of metal sticking up. This is a microphone, and through the magic of modem technology it brings his voice to me clearly. He does not need to shout.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
This government is very concerned with job creation. As a matter of fact, in the history of Canada it is the government which has created the largest number of jobs-one million and a half-which has improved productivity. True, after seven years of record growth the economy was over-heating; bungalows worth normally $80,000 were being sold for $300,000, $400,000; the economy was thrown off course. So we needed to act to prevent inflation from making it a continued reality.
To do that, you need to bring down the inflation pressure. And, Mr. Speaker, as you all know in this House that for-I do not know how many weeks, following each other, one after the other-the interest rates have been going down-again last week.

I wonder whether the minister can hear the cries of help from the people in the food bank line-ups and the people in the unemployment insurance line-ups.
I have a question for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. His government has frozen funding for medicare for two years, now for five years, yet the cost to the provinces for medicare are increasing at double the rate of inflation.
Oral Questions
Will the minister tell this House how he can expect anything from forthcoming provincial health budgets but hospital bed closures, lay-off of health care workers, cancellation of equipment purchases and cuts to all health services, none of which he can control by the Canada Health Act?
Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and
Welfare): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should be aware of the fact that over the next four years transfers to the provinces across the board will be increasing by some 3.7 per cent per year. We are asking the provinces to do nothing that we are not prepared to do even more stringently in areas under exclusive federal jurisdiction.
In terms of the amount of money involved in transfers to the provinces, the savings involved amount to about one half of 1 per cent of provincial revenues.
What I would ask the provinces to do is exactly what is being done by Ottawa; to look at priorities, to set priorities and to decide where they believe that money must most importantly be spent. Certainly health care is one of those key priorities. That is why we are committed to ensuring the existence of a national medicare program.

My question is for the Minister of Finance.
Robert Hamilton, executive director of the Hospital Association of Prince Edward Island, said last week that the measures to cut social spending in the budget could lead to bed closures, staff lay-offs and longer waits for surgery. Mr. Hamilton went on to say that Island hospitals have no more fat left to be cut.
Is the minister not aware that his budget is going to damage the quality of our health care system, not only in Prince Edward Island, but across the country?

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend has to balance the pressures on our health care systems, our education systems, as well as the pressures on the total finances of the country, federal, provincial and municipal. If we do not take the appropriate steps to get our deficits and our debts under control, then it is going to lead to much more lasting damage to both the economy as well as to

March 4, 1991
Oral Questions
these important programs. That is the essential direction the government took in the budget I delivered last week.
I met last night with the provincial finance ministers from across the country and we discussed these things. There was very strong agreement it was important that this government take the necessary steps to control the deficit and the debt for the simple reasons I have just elaborated.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister.
I have served in Prince Edward Island as provincial Minister of Health and Social Services. I know that the responsibilities of governing require tough choices. But I have to question the judgment and the sensitivity of any government that would try to reduce the deficit on the backs of the sick.
Hear, hear.
Mr. Speaker, why will this minister not admit that health care will be adversely affected by the measures taken in his budget?

Mr. Speaker, this is not what we have done. We have simply asked the provinces to accept a lower rate of growth, but a more significant rate of growth than what we are accepting for our own programs.
I told the provinces last night that we would be spending $183 billion over the next five years on transfers to the provinces. It is up to the provinces to decide where those moneys should be spent. Whether they are spent on health care, whether they are spent on post-secondary education, whether they are spent on highways or whether they are spent on salaries and wages of the people who work for the provincial governments, that is their choice. That is their jurisdiction.
Health care is a priority of this government. It has always been a priority and continues to be one.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Labour.
Given that this House voted in favour of restoring funding for the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety, and given the need for preventive health care services for workers, how can the minister justify slashing the centre's budget by another $110,000, adding insult to the $80,000 injury he inflicted on the CCOHS just last November?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Corbeil (Minister of Labour and Minister of State (TVansport)):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State (Transport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was delighted to hear that the hon. member for Hamilton West will be at the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety next week, since we are organizing a conference of occupational health and safety authorities, to stimulate public interest.
As far as the Budget is concerned, as the Minister of Finance just said, all federal ministers have been asked to do what they can to alleviate the enormous deficit a legacy of the government to which the hon. member belonged-and the $110,000 the Centre will be asked to cut from its overall budget of $11.5 million will, I am sure, be expertly absorbed by the centre's administrators who are competent people and who, I am sure, will find ways to continue to do their excellent work with the funds at their disposal.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the minister for his public service announcement for next week and ask the minister when the government is going to start taking responsibility for its own mistakes in policy when it comes to economics in this country.
I am not only speaking on my own here, but also for the president of the CCOHS. He is asking "that this government give us a break". That is his quote. Let us hold to the original terms of the agreement, he is asking.
This government must understand that by increasing funding and access to the centre, it will save money in the long run by promoting health care and safety for Canadian workers.
Injuries to workers costs Canada $29 billion every year. Because of the $1 billion cut to medicare, the government needs to address the issue of preventive health care.
March 4, 1991

Would the minister not agree that it would be in the best interests of Canadian workers to restore funding to the CCOHS?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Corbeil (Minister of Labour and Minister of State (Transport)):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State (Transport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recipe of the Liberals has been tried in this country for many years. Whenever there is a problem, they throw money at it and the problem disappears. This is not the philosophy of this government.
Over the years, we have fully supported the CCOHS. Every time they have asked us for bridge financing, we have given it. This year, we have asked the CCOHS to be equal to the other departments of this government and to find ways to continue doing an excellent job with a little less of financing. We are sure they are prepared and are capable of doing so.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thousands of forestry jobs in British Columbia and northern Ontario have been lost, due in part to the 1986 Memorandum of Understanding on the softwood lumber tariff.
Last week, the minister of trade met with B.C. Premier Vander Zalm to discuss a strategy to fight the tariff. In fact, representations are being made today in Washington, D.C. about the regressive impact that deal is having on Canada.
My question is for the Prime Minister. This tariff is a major trade irritant between Canada and the United States. I would like to ask the Prime Minister if he has raised this matter with President Bush and expressed Canada's concerns over this aspect of trade between our two countries.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the negotiations that the Minister for International Trade is carrying on are ongoing, both with provinces, premiers and ministers of trade from the various provinces as well as the United States.
There has been no decision, no conclusion as yet concerning these discussions but it is high on the agenda of the Minister for International Trade. He is continuing those negotiations.
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister.
In a news report today, for the first time the B.C. Minister of Forests is acknowledging some concern over Canada's sovereignty as it relates to forest policy.
Given these concerns about our political sovereignty, and in view of the fact that the U.S. administration has already asked and used the Memorandum of Understanding on the softwood tariff to question such internal decisions as the setting of Canadian freight rates for the transport of Canadian lumber products, will the minister advise this House what other Canadian policy decisions have been affected or questioned by United States authorities under the aegis of this Memorandum of Understanding?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
The Memorandum of Understanding was signed between the two governments and lays out very clearly the terms and conditions of that understanding.
There are areas where the United States has the right to look at certain charges and so on to make sure that the Memorandum of Understanding is being upheld. That is the same way as Canada would look at agreements with the United States and undertakings that they have taken such as questioning some of the subsidies they are providing for farmers today in the United States in competition with Canadian farmers.
We are questioning the agreement that they made with Canada. That goes on all the time. As I said earlier, the minister has this at the top of his list. He is in the process of negotiations with the provinces and will be discussing this with his counterpart in the United States in the veiy near future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Analysts with the Toronto Dominion Bank say that the Minister's Budget has an Alice in Wonderland perspective. Unfortunately, Canadians do not share the Minister of Finance's fairy-tale view of things.

March 4, 1991
Oral Questions
Now that Statistics Canada has announced that the composite leading indicator has dropped by 0.6 per cent and that the U.S. leading indicator has dropped 0.7 per cent, why won't the Minister of Finance admit that he has lost control of his made in Canada recession and why won't he introduce measures that will put Canadians back to work?

Mr. Speaker, I think the projections in my Budget are identical to those of the majority of economists in the private sector, i.e., the recession will end by the middle of this year and the economy will show an improvement of 3.5 per cent in the second half and also throughout next year. I think these projections are very realistic and that they are identical to those made by the majority of our economists.

Mr. Speaker, the minister forgets that the measures he took in his budget have actually changed the projections of some of the private sector economists.
But, in any event, I think Canadians want to know why the Minister of Finance seems to have a tendency to change his mind. Back in 1982, when he wanted to be Minister of Finance, he thought that the government's decision at that time during a recession to increase job creation programs by $500 million was, and I quote: "A step in the right direction, but a very small step". He clearly thought more should have been given.
In cutting $100 million from the Canadian Jobs Strategy, the minister should explain to Canadians why he no longer feels that the government should be helping to create jobs.

Mr. Speaker, there is a fundamental difference between the picture that we are looking at today and what we were looking at in 1982.
In 1982 there was a significantly less burden of debt on the federal government than is the case now. As I made very, very clear in the House last week, if we were to be increasing the size of the deficit, as I have heard my friend and his colleagues, plus colleagues from the New Democratic Party all saying, spend, spend, spend, what we would see is an increase in interest rates and that
increase in interest rates would do far more damage to the economy.
I should also point out to my friend that we are still very much committed on this side of the House to training and the importance of training to Canadian people, particularly to those out of a job. That is why we have transferred a considerable amount of the passive income support moneys in the unemployment insurance fund to active job training. It will amount to some $550 million in this current fiscal year, rising to about $750 million in the very near future.
So the commitment is very clearly there to help people get training.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. It concerns the administration of the national forum on Canada's future.
Last week, Mr. Robert Normand, a member of the forum, alleged that other commissioners were racking up scandalous bills for per diems and expenditures.
Now that these charges have been denied by the chairman over the weekend, will the Prime Minister, in the interest of protecting the integrity of his own forum, table immediately in the House of Commons a list of all disbursements, per diems and expenses paid to each member of the forum? If not, why not?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad to inform the hon. member that tomorrow, while tabling my Supplementary Estimates (C) for last year, he will have the numbers pertaining to that particular commission.
