speechtext: Each member?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Well, as the Prime Minister has indicated in this House before, there are procedures followed by these royal commissions. There are ways that these commissions have to be handled and need to be handled so that they maintain the autonomy that one desires them to have.
So I will be introducing that tomorrow and, of course, all of the expenditures will, in due course, be submitted to the auditor.
March 4, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I assume that on the weekend, the Prime Minister was able to consider the allegations made against the Spicer Commission, and my question is this: Could he give the House the assurance that he asked for and, in fact, received assurances that no irregularities had taken place? That is what we want to know.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I may remind the hon. member that the commission member who more or less started all this, if I am not mistaken, but who did so almost involuntarily-
He talked to his own reporter!

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
I think we should let people speak for themselves. It is very easy to make allegations, but Mr. Normand said that as far as he was concerned, he was going to stay.
In any case, there are a number of important rules, and I am sure the hon. member will realize that. When we set up a royal commission of inquiry, the government cannot start interfering and try to run the commission instead of the people who are there.
There are people on the commission like Mr. Normand and Mr. Spicer, and many other entirely responsible people, and I am sure they will see that the commission is properly run. In any case, tomorrow the amounts spent will be tabled and, at the appropriate time, the Auditor General will be able to review those expenditures and report to Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture, perhaps the Prime Minister could help me with the answer to this question, since we understand he was involved pretty directly four years ago with a similar problem in Saskatchewan or on the prairies.
The Canadian agriculture ministers met in Regina on the weekend to finalize the details of the government's farm income safety net program. We understand that they also discussed the emergency interim payments to
Oral Questions
farmers, allowing them to continue farming until GRIP and NISA are in place.
Can the Prime Minister confirm that the Canadian grain farmer will in fact receive an emergency cash payment or some other form of bankable commitment from the federal government this spring before seeding, and will the Prime Minister tell us what the amounts of this emergency payment will be?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
As my
colleague says, Mr. Speaker, the federal and provincial Ministers of Agriculture met in Regina on Friday and Saturday. Given the difficult agricultural situation they agreed on procedures to set up the two GRIP and NISA systems. Negotiations will continue over the next few days to finalize that part.
As to the rest, Mr. Speaker, before that long-term system can be set up to meet the needs of the farming community, the Minister of Agriculture said publicly that he would take temporary measures to help them. When the budget was tabled last week you saw that despite the difficult financial situation the government did manage to set aside an extra $1.3 billion for Canadian farmers. That is a commendable effort in these trying times and in the coming weeks we will decide how these funds are to be expended.

Mr. Speaker, my question specifically was whether or not that $1.3 million in the budget would be used for the cash emergency payment or a bankable commitment to the farmers before spring work. That means now.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
As it
has done over the past six years, Mr. Speaker, our government will come to the assistance of farm producers. But I would also remind my colleague that, as we did in recent years, we will see to it that the measures to be taken will have a long-term impact. As other members have pointed out, the days of carefree spending are over. Mr. Speaker, we have to be sure that program funding will solve the problem in the long term so that the neediest producers will get that money and stabilize their income for years to come. We will not be acting alone,

March 4, 1991
Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker, for we will seek the co-operation of the provinces, as we did in the past.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment. Since 1989 when the government unveiled the $250 million five-year federal-provincial shared-cost program, nothing has been signed by Ottawa and Quebec City to clean up the so-called orphan sites at Joutel, Cadillac, Dupar-quet and others in Quebec. My question is this: Since you have been appointed we know you are prepared to sign that agreement in the interest of the people of Quebec, so is the Quebec government prepared to enter into a Canada-Quebec agreement concerning the so-called orphan contaminated sites?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
As a government, Mr. Speaker, we concluded the negotiations with Quebec at the end of last November. We have the draft of a bilateral agreement which has been approved by my provincial counterpart and which was submitted to the various committees of the Quebec cabinet for approval. We have every indication that Quebec is prepared to sign the agreement by the end of this month.
Therefore I am hopeful that the agreement will be in force within a few weeks.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
While the minister was out propagandizing and promoting her new immigration strategy program, the reality is that the English language training programs for new immigrants across Canada are being undermined and dismantled. In Manitoba, over 2,100 immigrants presently enrolled in the English language training program are now having those positions put in jeopardy
by the change in federal funding and the lay-off of close to 68 teachers.
Rather than this kind of dismantling and restructuring, will the minister meet with her Manitoba colleague, the provincial minister, to restore the existing funding so that the 2,100 immigrants who are presently in language training programs will not have them jeopardized and have them ended at the end of this month.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the money we have put into language training has over time been increased. Actually, we are doing a lot more by way of settlement and teaching of language than was done by the former government, as the hon. member well knows. We will continue that commitment to make as much available as we can under the current economic conditions and by doing it in less expensive ways, moving through NGOs and other organizations which can deliver the service more effectively.

Mr. Speaker, as the minister well knows, if you do not have a job or if you do not presently speak the language, you do not qualify for those programs. There are thousands of new immigrants who are not eligible for the minister's new programs. They cannot learn the language, therefore, they cannot get a job. If they cannot get a job, they cannot get into the program. It is a total catch-22.
Considering how generous the minister has been in the funding of language programs in other provinces, will she not at least consider restoring the funding in the province of Manitoba so that the people who are presently getting training under those conditions can have their rights restored and can go on and become valuable members of our society?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government does provide language training for people who are not destined for the labour force. I would remind him that we are the first government to have done so. In terms of where the dollars go across Canada, they are spent in the regions as they are required. This department and this minister have been stronger on language and settlement programs than, I think it is fair to say, any former government and, certainly, other Liberal ministers.
March 4, 1991

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
While the new Terminal 3 at Pearson airport is operating, it is completely irresponsible and unacceptable for this government to continue to have a veil of secrecy surround the entire deal that this government signed with the private consortium.
I ask the minister, since every Canadian taxpayer has a full legitimate right to know every single detail about the agreement, to inform this House how much of a profit the private consortium is expected to make. What is the share of that proposed profit with the federal government? Will the Canadian taxpayer ever be expected to pick up any shortfall during the duration of this sweet agreement with the private consortium?

Mr. Speaker, in February 1988, the media and all MPs, I believe, were provided with a press kit. I quote from that press kit: "There is going to be a $2 million payment to Transport Canada on signing the ground phase. A further $28 million was paid on the opening of the terminal. Transport Canada receives, on a sliding scale, 3 to 5 per cent of gross revenue for the first five years, plus $1 million minimum guarantee", and so on.
All that information was made available three years ago. I am surprised it has taken my friend this long to catch up with it.

Mr. Speaker, the minister continues to stonewall. While he may be able to read a press release, he is having trouble listening to the questions that are being asked on this side of the House.
I return to the minister on a different matter concerning the same agreement. The minister has admitted that the government made a serious error in dealing away the rights of limousines and taxis to the private consortium in the agreement.
Can the minister confirm that the government has negotiated, or is currently negotiating, to buy back that particular clause; and if so, what is the expected price tag to the Canadian taxpayer for this monumental blunder made by this Minister of Transport?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I never at any time admitted that we made a blunder with respect to the taxis. When we got into taxi and limousine service, I made it very clear that I wanted every traveller passing through Pearson International Airport to get the same service at all three terminals. That is what we have decided to do, and we have renegotiated it so that that will occur. I am sure that all travellers going through Terminal 3 especially-the terminal that the Liberals do not like-will enjoy it very much.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and relates to allegations made by Mr. Normand, editor at Le Soleil, regarding the Spicer Commission. They call for immediate action, especially after Mr. Spicer stated yesterday that the Canadian people could not care less about how the Spicer Commission is administered.
Mr. Speaker, how can the Prime Minister remain silent after such allegations were made by his friend, Mr. Normand, and after $25 million were squandered to pay the members of the commission $18,000 each per 30-day period when in fact they work only five or six days? Will the Prime Minister commit before this House to ask Mr. Spicer to resign, to adjourn the proceedings and to institute immediately an inquiry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member just the same for his concern for this Commission and thus, I imagine, the future of this country.
Regarding the management of the Spicer Commission, Mr. Normand brought out some important finer points. I would caution the hon. member against making somewhat unfounded assertions. In any case, I will remind the House-I was taking for granted that everyone was aware-that commissions such as this one is subject to certain rules, generally Treasury Board regulations on hiring, contracts, rental. They work under what I would call soft supervision because they need to maintain some autonomy. I am sure the hon. member will be bitterly disappointed when he finds out, as the Auditor General will reveal, that everything was done properly after all.

March 4, 1991
Privilege

Mr. Speaker, is the President of the Treasury Board telling this House that the Spicer Commission was given a blank cheque and that there is no concern about what is going on, at a time when an additional load is put on the Canadian people and a crippling blow is sent to the neediest as well as to smokers and when the UI premiums are going up? Is that your vision of national unity?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: That is not what I said at all. If that is what the hon. member heard, he heard wrong. Quite the contrary, I said that there are rules for managing Royal commission enquiries. We do not have a laisser-faire policy. There are rules, but they allow a measure of autonomy. That is not only necessary but desirable, as I think everyone will agree. As for the rest, the rules followed by the Spicer Commission in the adjudication of contracts across the country to respond to its needs are based on Treasury Board standards, as I am sure all this will be confirmed in due course. Tomorrow, when the Estimates (C) are presented, the last ones for the current year, that is 1990-1991, you will see what amounts are involved.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister.
Five years ago today, his government responded to the unanimous report of the Special Committee on Equality Rights by promising to take whatever measures are necessary to ensure that sexual orientation is a prohibited ground of discrimination in all areas of federal jurisdiction. The government has failed for five years now to live up to that commitment, including a fresh commitment made by the Minister of Justice at this time last year.
Members of Parliament have received many letters on this matter, and I want to ask the Prime Minister: When the government will live up to that commitment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)

Mr. Speaker, I think that the hon. member is aware that my predecessor, the then President of the TVeasury Board, came forward with a very valid proposal which we consider to be fair, a proposal which was established in full consultation with Public Service unions. We feel that we stand on good ground.
This was appealed to a board. Therefore I cannot discuss its value. We will wait for the decision of this tribunal and, when it comes, we will see where we are at that time.

The question of privilege is that I have attempted to communicate as a member of Parliament with Mr. Kealey. He is now behind barriers-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

March 4, 1991

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I indicated to the hon. member that I was going to have to be fairly definite with respect to this particular matter.
The hon. member knows that as a consequences of the hostilities there were barriers put up in order to maintain crowd control and security at the immediate doors of the buildings of Parliament.
As I understand it, and from what I have read in the paper, for whatever reason Mr. Kealey got into some difficulties with respect to those barriers.
However, there is nothing that has indicated that Mr. Kealey or anybody else cannot demonstrate on the other side of those barriers and within relatively close proximity to the buildings, but the hon. member has to persuade me-and I am afraid he is not going to be able to-that somehow whatever has happened to Mr. Kealey infringes his privileges or the privileges of other hon. members.
I think that the hon. member's complaint, whatever it may be, does fall short of privilege. The hon. member, of course, can pursue this at Question Period at another time if he wishes.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
No, I am not taking a point of order to extend the point of privilege. I think the hon. member has made his point. I have to indicate to him again that I do not see this as a question of privilege.
I think the hon. member may very well have a complaint, but there must be another way to bring it to the attention of the House.
The hon. member on a point of order.

Of course I respect the Speaker's rulings completely, but I do feel that I never really had a chance to at least offer, perhaps in one or two sentences, what I thought was my point because of some loud heckling-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member again. I understand perfectly well what the hon. member's point is. It is not a point of privilege. It may well be a complaint.
I do know what it is, and it was not because of any noise on the other side of the House. It is not a question of privilege. I am not hearing it further.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to present again a petition. It is one on behalf of the volunteer firemen of Canada. As you may or may not know-and you probably do not if you live in an urban centre-rural areas depend very often on volunteer firemen.
They serve a very useful purpose. They are not paid a lot. In some cases they are not paid at all, but one way is to issue them with an income tax receipt. They get one for $400. That was raised back over 10 years ago from $300 to $400 and has not been raised since.

speechtext: When the debate was interrupted, the hon. member for Ottawa South had the floor. The hon. member has 17 minutes left, and he may now proceed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives alone are responsible for failing to control the public debt during seven years of unprecedented economic growth; for having on more than 30 occasions levied regressive taxes on taxpayers who were already
March 4, 1991

strapped financially; for managing to create a made-in-Canada recession; for practically strangling employment opportunities in the manufacturing sector as a result of their policy of maintaining high interest rates and a high dollar; for introducing the GST, an expensive and very complex tax both for small business and for consumers.

Since 1984, the Conservatives have attempted to convince Canadians that only they could successfully manage the public purse. But, after almost seven years in office, during which Canada has shared with the rest of the western economies almost unprecedented economic growth and despite having resorted to over 30 different tax increases paid largely by middle and lower income Canadians, the Minister of Finance has failed in bringing the deficit under control. In fact he has managed to double the federal debt while at the economic controls.
The minister is always eager to talk about the bad old Liberals who supposedly started the problem. This is typical of a government that never seems able to take responsibility for anything. The deficit? Blame the Liberals. Interest rates? Those are the fault of those crazy consumers and their excessive credit demands. Inflation? That is caused by the Public Service wage increases. National unit? Blame that one on the Leader of the Opposition. Whatever the problem, it is someone else's fault.
When is this government going to grow up and start accepting responsibility for the problems that it has created? Surely, after seven years in office, the government now owns the deficit. The debt was below $200 billion when the Tories were elected in 1984. Soon it will exceed $400 billion. The only thing that this government has finally admitted is that Canada is now in a recession and that the recession was induced by government policy.
The Conservatives' home-made recession is no ordinary downturn in the economy. As a direct result of policies pursued by the government, job producing industries have been driven out of business and in many cases driven right out of the country, never to return. Many of the 288,000 jobs that were lost between April of 1990 and January of this year are lost for good. People in
The Budget
other countries are now employed in jobs that until recently provided a means of livelihood for Canadians.
To make matters worse, the imposition of the costly and administratively complex goods and services tax has taken more money directly out of people's wallets and made life more difficult for small businesses.
This budget should have offered Canadians some reason for optimism, hope and vision.

This Budget should have provided a sound basis for getting Canada out of its economic hornets nest and getting Canadians to work. Nowhere in the Budget is there any indication of how this government intends to help Canadians.

In the 1988 election campaign the Prime Minister claimed that to elect the Liberals would put Canada's economic growth in jeopardy. I quote:
The damage of a Liberal win to economic activity in southern Ontario would be swift, dramatic and powerful.
He also said:
Earlier in this decade Canadians suffered through the worst recession in post-war history. Do Canadians want to risk a return to that?
By electing a Conservative government Canadians got more than a risk of recession; they got the real thing.
But the most damning thing about this budget is the lack of hope for the million and a half jobless who, with their families, are the real victims of this recession.
Despite predictions of economic recovery in the second half of this year and strong growth in 1992, the jobless rate is not going to improve by the government's own predictions. There is nothing in the budget about job creation. There is only a cut of $100 million from the Canadian Jobs Strategy, and there is the implicit acceptance of an unemployment rate of almost 10 per cent.
When he was in opposition, the Minister of Finance understood the importance of keeping people at work. For example, in 1982 he said:
The government must begin to realize that it is individual people who are being hurt. It is not the political game that we are playing here in the House of Commons that is important; we must deal with the real

March 4, 1991
The Budget
world. We cannot stay here in an ivory tower in Ottawa; we must deal
with individual Canadians who are losing their jobs and businesses.
Further he said:
-when people are struggling for survival, when people fear that they will lose their jobs or that their children cannot find that first job, there is not much trust and generosity. Rhetoric will not produce the harmony we all want, but a healthy economy will.
If only the Minister of Finance still believed those same principles. He has produced a budget of no jobs, a budget of no hope, and a budget of no vision.
The government in the past has talked a lot about creating the conditions for economic growth. Even in this budget, the indication is that all that needs to be done is to lower inflation and bring down the deficit and economic growth will follow. But these measures alone will not bring economic growth and prosperity.
Without a strong sense of national consensus and the force of national will, Canada's future prosperity is not ensured. The failure of the Mulroney government to promote national unity is closely linked to the severity of the problems confronting us on the economic front.
At a time when national consensus has never been more essential and possibly never harder to achieve, the government's cuts to transfer payments and Canada Assistance Plan payments will only further aggravate stresses on Canadian unity.
The Allaire report in Quebec includes an attack on the federal imposition of national standards, while simultaneously withdrawing federal financial support. Because such criticism is not unfounded, the erosion of national standards and the corresponding sense of nationhood may well result.

The Tories heavily penalized the provinces by reducing transfer payments, and they deceived Canadians. However, Canadians are well aware there is only one taxpayer: the Canadian taxpayer, who pays all taxes, whether they are federal, provincial or municipal.

Shifting the deficit from the federal level to the provincial level does nothing for the over-all economic well-being of the nation. If anything, it is the steady
withdrawal of the national government from so many aspects of Canadian life that is causing Canadians in Quebec and other regions to begin to question whether Canada is really worth the struggle any more.
Then there is the attack on labour in general and the government's own employees in particular. The budget proposal to impose a freeze on Public Service wage budgets typifies the approach of this cynical government to try to pin the blame for inflation on a group of Canadians which the government thinks will gamer little public sympathy across Canada; this after boasting that the federal government had been keeping Public Service wages below inflation in past years.
According to Labour Canada, federal government workers' wage settlements were 5.3 per cent in 1990 compared to 5.9 per cent in the private sector and 5.6 per cent in other public sectors. Where is the flexibility that the Minister of Finance himself demanded back in 1982 when he said that there should be different treatment for low income employees and those who merit some increased remuneration because of good work.
This attack on the Public Service will result, I predict, in a further deterioration of service to Canadians who rely on federal programs and services. The delivery of income supplements, the provision of air traffic control services, the processing of immigration and refugee claims and so and so on. Canadians can expect that these services will continue to deteriorate as the government induces the best of its employees to leave the Public Service and increases the work load on those that remain.
It has been said that in a democracy the people get the government they deserve. I do not believe that Canadians are getting what they deserve from this government. Canadians deserve from their government a financial plan that demonstrates a commitment to invest in our most important resource; our people. This entails not just support for post-secondary education but for continuing training and retraining for adult workers, ensuring that Canada's workforce is versatile enough to face the challenges of globalization.
This would address our growing people deficit. Instead of living up to his self-proclaimed title, "the education
March 4, 1991

Prime Minister", this Prime Minister has reduced transfers to the provinces in support of post-secondary education four times since 1984.
A responsible government would have demonstrated a strategy to deal with the fact that at least 90,000 of
180,000	manufacturing jobs lost during this recession are permanently removed from the Canadian economy according to Laurent Thibault, president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. Such a strategy would address our widening science and technology deficit.
A wise government would have shown Canadians that it understood the relationship between the quality of a nation's transportation and communication infrastructure and the share of the world's wealth it will possess. A caring government would have offered hope to its unemployed that they will get back to work. Instead the Conservative approach to a job strategy consists of a $100 million cut from the Canadian Jobs Strategy.

What does the Budget have to offer Canadians who lost their jobs because government policies forced their employers to move elsewhere? What does this Budget have to say about the government's role in ensuring that Canadians are competitive on world markets? What does this Budget and its predecessors have to say about the value this government sets on education, research, development, training and development? What message does this government have for entrepreneurs who have the knowhow to increase productivity but lack the capital?

Perhaps the most succinct and damaging critique of the budget of all is that contained in the budget analysis provided by the Toronto Dominion Bank. They say: "The main problem of this budget is that it addresses none of Canada's major economic problems".
Very simply in conclusion, this is a budget of no jobs, no hope, no vision, but more pain. Truly the emperor has no clothes.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened as usual with great interest to my colleague's speech.
In listening to the budget debate of members of the opposition from both parties-not only from the Liberals but from the New Democratic Party as well-I cannot
The Budget
help but hear a message loud and clear that the government should be spending money and spending more money and spending more money. Not once in any of the speeches do I hear that the government should live within its means.
The hon. member said there is no message in the budget. There is one very clear message in the budget; if we as a country are going to survive, if we as a country are going to continue to provide the programs that are so necessary and that the public wants, then somewhere along the line a government has to take cognizance of the expenditures and the income and the amount of money being borrowed.
Liberal members of Parliament talk a great game. They have picked programs one after another that should be supported with more money. The hon. member talks about cutting here and cutting there. This government has done that, has made it very clear that we are transferring one-third of the income of the federal government to the provinces, and we have a financial problem, they are part of that problem and they have to be part of the solution.
I want to ask the hon. member a very direct question, because he is one of the financial critics of the Liberal Party. We know what they are against. We understand fully that they want money thrown at this, that or the other thing. I have a couple of specific questions. The first is, are you concerned about the deficit of this country? Second, what would the Liberals-if they were ever elected-do about the deficit and how would they cut that deficit? I would like to hear some positive suggestions from the Liberals which, to this time in this debate, have not been forthcoming.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy these exchanges with the Minister of State for Privatization. I must say that I am pleased that there are ministers here for this debate today. It is regrettable that when the finance critic for the opposition spoke, he spoke to a Chamber devoid of ministers.
The question is an important one and I acknowledge that these are issues which need to be addressed by parties on all sides of the House. I take exception to the characterization, of course, that the minister has put both on my remarks and on the remarks of some of my colleagues because clearly, if he had been listening he

March 4, 1991
The Budget
would have understood my concern about the deficit and the debt.
He is well aware of what the deficit was in 1984 when he was elected and how the present Minister of Finance managed to run it up before the end of the first fiscal year in which he was in office so as to establish an extremely high base from which to then describe his later reductions. He is also aware that after seven years of growth in the Canadian economy, the annual deficit continues to be over $30 billion a year. He is aware that the Minister of Finance this weekend, in an interview with Southam News, acknowledged that he had made the wrong policy choice in 1987 when he introduced tax reductions, thereby contributing to the deficit, instead of being honest with the people of Canada and facing the deficit before the election. So he has managed to build it up into a bigger problem than it should be.
I would suggest to the minister, if he wants to seriously make some progress on this, two things. Before he looks too hard and long at what programs to cut, he needs to look at how he is building for the future. What kind of country are we going to have in the future and how are we going to meet the challenges of the future? Any good businessman knows that if he is going to meet the challenges to come sometimes he has to borrow to invest.
What this government does not make a distinction about is the difference between spending and investing. In cutting investing, they are really cutting its lifeline for the future. When it fails to meet the spending requirements for education, for infrastructure, for science and technology, it is really hurting our ability in the years to come to meet the requirements that Canada will have in order to compete in the global economy.
All of that being said, I wonder why it is that this government seems to have money to move operations of government without gaining any particular efficiency. In this budget it has decided to throw millions of dollars at moving the National Energy Board. Now, there may be good reasons for that on an operational level, but we do not know of any particular reason why at a time of recession it needs to throw that money in. We know they have almost $250 million to build a space agency in St. Hubert, when the same functions are being carried on
quite well without that expenditure being made. They do not seem to be willing to cut back.
We know that they have ministers of state with limousines that sat outside here on budget night, burning gasoline. I suspect that the minister who posed the question was not included in the number of people who let his limousine sit out there idling, but others did. It is an outrage and it is a disgrace. Why not cut back the number of ministers of state? There is a suggestion for you. Why not look at the tax expenditure account and see what tax expenditures can either be reduced or, perhaps, postponed. Maybe that is too innovative an approach for the government.
Why does the government insist on a cumbersome and lengthy refugee review process to actually effect the elimination of very few false refugees from Canada? It spends close to $100 million a year in order to eliminate a couple of hundred people from Canada. Why is the government not looking at any of these suggestions?
Why is it that the level of corporate profits over the last number of years has remained at roughly the same percentage of gross domestic profit? In spite of that, why is it the contribution of corporate income tax to the government revenues has gone down? Why is it that the percentage of income in the upper income category, while remaining the same, has seen a lower burden of income tax, looked at as a percentage of GDP on one side and as government revenue on the other?
I cannot answer these questions for the government, perhaps they can.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, the answer is to cut about $10 million of expenditures, as he is suggesting in his speech, for a $30 billion deficit. That was his suggestion. Also he suggests we increase the deficit because he said we should borrow more. I heard him say that. We should borrow more. We should invest in the future.
The Liberals tried that. They borrowed $16 billion in 1984 just for programs, not to service the debt or anything else, just for programs. This government now has a surplus in program spending. We collect more than we spend on programs. We have a huge deficit to service.

The hon. member talks about the deficit increasing. That is right. But all from interest payable on the huge debt that we inherited. I remember what it was when we took over. It was $200 billion. I remember it very clearly.
I want to understand the hon. member perfectly. He wants to borrow more at this particular time and increase the deficit. That is exactly what he said.
I want to ask him one other question. His leader, who I am pleased to learn is coming along well and is feeling much better and will be back with us soon, has been reported as saying he would cut the universality in social programs to save money. I wonder if that, in fact, is Liberal policy? Is it a suggestion from the Liberal Party that the new leader of the party made recently? It was reported that he is prepared to change the universality of those programs in order to cut the deficit?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all let me say that I do not think the minister is adding up my numbers very accurately, if he has only come to the number he referred to. I think I suggested to him that he could even save almost $100 million on the refugee program alone, if he were to redirect the intention of the government on that.
The point is, in listening to this government, if their financial methods were applied in private business, Robert Campeau would still be in business today, because his only problem was that he could not cover his debt charges. But these people have been in office for seven years. They have been in office longer than it took to defeat Adolf Hitler in World War II, and they are still coming out crying about the deficit after all the time they have had to confront it and fight it.
I think it is time for them to surrender and let somebody else take on the battle.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald S. Merrithew (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate because I want to very clearly state my position on Canada's economic future.

I am pleased to take part in this budget debate, Mr. Speaker, because this is a rather historic occasion. It is a
The Budget
time for elected officials to stand before their constituents, and the country, and declare where they stand on Canada's economic future.

I stand unequivocally behind the plan for economic recovery delivered in the House of Commons last week by my colleague the Minister of Finance. It is a blueprint for renewed prosperity and economic growth.
It recognizes that Canada must continue to sit at the table with other industrialized nations as an equal. Today, international capital travels along a fibre-optic cable seeking the best country in which to invest. The budget continues to lay the groundwork commenced in 1984 by the same Minister of Finance for making Canada an envied investment location in the international marketplace.
How exactly are these noble goals to be achieved? One, reducing the annual deficit and the national debt, two, eliminating our need to borrow on foreign markets, three, reducing inflation, and four, reducing interest rates are the keys to creating an economic environment where Canadians can prosper.
This budget, this plan for economic recovery, will do all of those things. It establishes targets for inflation. It will cast in the laws of the land limits to the government expenditure growth. It will create the Debt Serving and Reduction Fund, a tangible example to all Canadians that we are serious when we say that this deficit will be eliminated. If the government of Canada ignores the deficit, disregards the debt, and throws a bucketful of money at our problems in an effort to buy our way out of this recession, we will all be sorry.
Living beyond our means is a recipe for disaster. It will return us to an era called by a well-respected journalist "the nightmare years", the years between 1975 and 1984, when a profligate, fat and wasteful federal government spent its way into the mess Canadians currently endure. No longer can Canadians wilfully spend dollars they have not earned and expect our children and our grandchildren to pay it back.
Of crucial importance is the decision to place government finances on the road to a balanced budget. The operations of government will be restrained. The Canadian people must know that we are doing our share. We have the responsibility of leading Canada; we therefore

March 4, 1991
The Budget
must lead by example. In fact, a recent poll suggested that 70 per cent of Canadians recognize and support the need to reduce government spending and to reduce the deficit.
And now a bit about my own portfolio. I see that we have one veteran in the House today. My portfolio cares for a very special group of men and women: Canada's war veterans. One in three males over the age of 65 in Canada is a veteran. There are more than 38,000 female veterans. They constitute a sizeable and influential component of this country. Altogether, Canada still has almost 600,000 veterans of World Wars I and II and Korea. They have done their part for Canada, and we are now returning their favour. So, I say to all veterans today that your valuable programs are untouched by this budget. Our level of commitment to you is undiminished. Canada will continue to have the most generous and compassionate veterans' programs and benefits of any country in the world. Do not let the critics make you think otherwise.
In my portfolio, we have viewed the fiscal constraint as an opportunity, a management challenge. It provides an opportunity to improve our efficiency, to re-evaluate the way we do business, and to identify ways that we can enhance our service. In Veterans Affairs Canada we will without a doubt rise to any challenge that confronts us.
Some hon. members may have read a recent report published by the C. D. Howe Institute in Toronto that implied our department was costly and administratively inefficient. The media picked up the story and the word spread. It was a message of course in direct disagreement with the corporate culture at Veterans Affairs Canada. That report was wrong.
I cannot and will not allow such statements to circulate without challenging them, which I did. Unchallenged, these claims do a disservice to our hard working staff and are unfair to our valued clients. The President of the C. D. Howe Institute personally apologized to me and to the department. Recently in the Vancouver Sun the author admitted she was wrong.
For the record, administrative costs at the Department of Veterans Affairs are less than 10 per cent of the total cost. Ninety-one point seven per cent of our budget will be delivered in the form of economic support and health
care directly to our veterans. We are surely one of the leanest operations in government.
The plan for economic recovery as laid out in the 1991 federal budget establishes the framework for government operations for years to come. It is the new reality and we are ready for it.
In addition to my portfolio responsibilities, I continue to have a strong and a passionate commitment to Atlantic Canada's regional development. For my home province of New Brunswick, the plan for economic recovery announced last week will be an important economic development tool, a stepping stone to renewed economic prosperity and growth.
I prefer to think that the Minister of Finance presented not a budget to Canadians, but a blueprint for the future.

I am committed to the belief that the best regional development tool is a lower deficit, a lower national debt, lower inflation and lower interest rates. A truly competitive national economy demands these things.

Lower deficit, lower interest, lower debt, lower inflation, lower interest rates, those are the items that we need for regional economic development in Canada. A truly competitive national economy creates opportunities, economic and otherwise, for all Canadians living in all regions in this country.
This new era of fiscal responsibility which we started in 1984 has an especially pronounced impact upon our relationship with the provinces. Because this debt is a national problem, it will demand national solutions. All levels of government must learn to live within their means and the tide of rising expectations of what governments at all levels are capable of doing must be tempered.
Governments must be imaginative and ingenious in how they use the resources that they do have. Just as the average Canadian must pay the bills, so must all levels of government.
The 1991 plan for economic recovery restrains the growth of transfers to the provinces. It limits this growth to an average of 3.7 per cent per year. Meanwhile federal government program spending will be limited to just 3 per cent annual growth. So you see, Mr. Speaker, we are
March 4, 1991

not asking from the provinces any more than what we ask of ourselves.
In New Brunswick, my home province, this economic blueprint is most encouraging. There are no caps on transfers to my province from the Canada Assistance Plan. There are no caps on the equalization payments to the province of New Brunswick. The per capita cap in the Established Programs Financing payments to provinces was announced in last year's budget and will continue for a further three years.
Since transfer payments constitute 20 per cent of all federal program spending, it is reasonable that they too must reflect prudent constraint. Let me put this in perspective. Federal transfers to New Brunswick represent 39 per cent of that province's revenues. Transfers are expected to increase at a yearly rate of more than 4 per cent. The CAP and EPF, Established Programs Financing transfers will account for only .2 per cent, that is two-tenths of one per cent, of the provincial revenues in 1992-93 in my province of New Brunswick.
The impact upon the provinces is negligible. Any protests to the contrary are being deceitful. Any complaints that the province will be unable to afford quality health care and education is untrue. Worse, it is fear-mongering. It is taking advantage of the frailties and the uncertainties of the poorest and least educated citizens.
I believe that the premier of New Brunswick is in full support of our plan for economic renewal. In a recent speech delivered in Toronto, Premier McKenna stated:
-borrowing money on current account is a fool's game. The leader of today enjoys the popularity of dispensing bought favours. The leader of tomorrow must devote all of his or her energy and ambition to paying the bills.
Premier McKenna goes on to say:
- the leaders of the 60s and 70s have placed a first mortgage on the future of Canada. The leaders of the 80s and 90s are placing a second mortgage on the same asset. There is no equity left. We must once and for all put an end to the suffocating debt-load we are placing on the backs of our children.
It is gratifying to see that a Liberal premier is not enamoured with the notion that government spending cures all ills. Premier McKenna is not the only Liberal premier who shares these views.
The Budget
Governments at all levels must treat their financial dealings in exactly the same manner as the average Canadian citizen must do. Like any householder, we should only borrow for big ticket items like our homes or major appliances, but on a day-to-day basis we must pay as we go.
The major difficulty the Canadian government faces today is that we must pay 36 cents on every dollar that we take in just to pay the interest on money previous governments borrowed in the past. For the provinces that figure is 11 cents on the dollar. We are strangling ourselves with debt and if we continue bad financial management, governments at all levels, like ordinary citizens, will face bankruptcy.
Many Canadians fail to comprehend the serious situation we are in today because of bad spending practices in previous times. Well, Canada has a huge collective debt burden totalling almost $400 billion. As most people find difficulty in comprehending such enormous sums, let me clarify what this means in simpler terms.
It means that every man, woman and child in Canada owes as part of the federal debt about $15,000. If we add on the collective debts of all the provincial and the municipal governments, then each and every Canadian owes about $20,000 for past profligate spending by previous governments at all levels.
Truly, we have spent money we have not earned and this practice cannot continue. To do so threatens the economic and financial future of those we love so dearly, our families and, indeed, their families.
Ordinary Canadians have a difficult time comprehending what a billion dollars represents, let alone our cumulative debt of $400 billion. What we all do know is that it must be paid back just as ordinary Canadians have to pay back money they borrowed in the past.
Let me explain the enormity of the problem that 26 million Canadians face in paying off our $400 billion debt. If Canada had set aside each and every day $500,000 since the birth of Christ, we would still not have enough money to pay off our public debt.
This budget recognizes the horrendous debt problem Canada faces if it continues down the road to uncontrolled spending-an annual deficit reduction.

March 4, 1991
The Budget
Opposition members and others suggest we should have more make-work projects and spend even more money we have not earned. They would have us spend our way out of the recession. Well, previous governments tried this and it simply did not work. It only compounds our deficit and debt problems by adding more debts which we will expect our children to pay.
I fully support the 1991 federal budget which will inevitably control inflation and subsequently bring what this country really needs-lower interest rates. The budget will set out clear, achievable inflation targets, reaching a low of 2 per cent by the mid-1990s. The budget will put government finances firmly on a course to a balanced budget. The budget will severely restrain the operations of our own government, as a model to be followed by provincial and municipal governments. The very best thing we can do as Canadians is to set this country on the road to economic and fiscal recovery. A strong and competitive economy means prosperity, and prosperity in Canada means wealth creation and new jobs for our people.
To fail to set Canada along this path to prosperity is to fail in our responsibilities. I have no intention of abrogating my responsibilities as a parliamentarian, and therefore I will be supporting this 1991 economic recovery plan.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very intently to the hon. minister's reply to the speech on the budget. I listened as he talked about the need for us to pay our bills and to reduce the debt. I cannot say that I agree with him totally on everything he said; there are some concerns I do have in listening to him speak about one of the particular areas within the area he is responsible for.
I know and hope that the veterans of this country will not bear any burden as a result of the steps taken and those going to be taken by this budget.
I have had much correspondence in the last number of months from veterans' groups and veterans individually about Veterans Affairs Canada. One question they asked was, what is the future of it? I know the minister has spoken on the budget debate and I would like to put that question to him.
The future of the Department of Veterans Affairs has caused great concern in some areas. Rumours have been circulating, of course, for a number of years. This is nothing new.
I would like to pose the same question in a different manner than I did the other afternoon, and this is regarding the veterans of the just-concluded war in the Persian Gulf, as to their benefits. There was one area of concern to me and that is the availability of housing for these veterans. I know that veterans of other wars were able to qualify for housing. It was a great way for these people to obtain houses.
I wonder if the minister could reply as to whether the government is looking into this in any way, making these people who have served in the gulf able to qualify for these houses. I know the Veterans Land Act has been wound down in the last year, but I wonder if he could inform me and this House today, if there is a possibility that these people will be eligible and, therefore, would be able to say that, yes, these people are going to receive the same benefits as all other veterans of wars.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In response to the hon. member for Hillsborough, he asked two questions. I would like to address the first one; what does the future hold for Veterans Affairs Canada?
Naturally, it has been 45 years or better since the end of the second war and about 40 years or 35 years since the end of the Korean War. One might think that as our veterans pass on, and the hon. member knows that the average age is 70 years of age, that all of a sudden the work of the department would be decreasing. Quite the contrary is true.
As veterans get older the kinds of problems, the aches and pains and the hardships they endured during those times in fighting for our country have now come home to roost, if you will, and very often they are in more need, in fact they are in significantly more need, as they grow older. They need more health care. They need more home care.
Let me put that in perspective. During the month of January, and the hon. member for Hillsborough will appreciate this, my department and the Canadian Pension Commission in Charlottetown handled 2,200 cases of first decisions. That set a record in history for the number of first decisions made by the Canadian Pension Commission. I think it is an indication that while the numbers may be declining, and that is true, the problems
March 4, 1991

and the health care problems that these veterans have are increasing.
Naturally, I cannot comment on the future of the department. The Prime Minister, the agency of government, the machinery of government will look at those kinds of things. Certainly I do not feel that my job, and I am sure my department does not feel that our job, is getting any easier. In fact, with the kind of new programs that we have brought in, particularly the Veterans Independence Program, and TAPS, and many of the other programs our jobs are getting even harder.
On the second point, I guess we can thank God that the war has finished in the gulf-we hope it has-and that Canadians can return home. We can take some comfort in the fact that Canada suffered no casualties in that conflict, despite the fact that we had 2,500 people there, some of whom were at the sharp point.
Let us first analyse the nature of the people who are serving. This is not like the Second World War where we had 1.1 million Canadians, basically civilians. It was a volunteer army who came out of the factories and out of the fields in Canada and formed the Canadian active service force. These people were going immediately at the cessation of war in 1945 right back into civilian life, unlike the service people who are fighting in the gulf today. They are professional servicemen and servicewomen. They will go directly back into the service and will, therefore, be assured of all the benefits and services that they get from Canada's armed forces which are very, very significant and indeed, much better than what was given to them in the Second World War and to veterans subsequently.
The hon. member asked particularly if we are going to provide the benefits. Yes, we are. We are going to provide significantly all of the benefits. The two big ones that count the most of, course, are disability pensions and treatment services for those people who might have had a disability incurred while serving in a special duty area like the gulf.
The housing aspect is quite different now than after the Second World War when previous governments wanted to do something very significant for those veterans who gave up such a big piece of their life to fight in World War II. There was a definite program to set up more veterans housing.
The Budget
This time these people are coming back to their old service jobs. Of course, there will not be the need to set up special programs, but that does not mean that we do not have veterans housing. We have a lot of veterans' housing. I think in my home city of Saint John, New Brunswick, that we have the largest number of veterans' housing units in Canada. Those will continue. There are new ones being opened at various times. We just opened one in Winnipeg, one in British Columbia and, of course, there are a number of Legions and other non-profit groups that want to do things for our veterans. I think we are doing fairly well by that.
The need is not quite there like it was when our vets returned home from World War II.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very important time in Parliament because it is one of those debates in which the people of Canada have an opportunity to be heard.
Perhaps one of the most important responsibilities of any member of Parliament is to use this budget debate as the occasion when he can express the hopes, fears, concerns, anxieties and attitudes of his own constituents. The one thing the budget does is crystallize those views and gives people a sense of what the blueprint for their lives will be for the future.
Over the last four or five days, in talking to people in my riding, this is a time when their voices have a certain common and disturbing ring to them. There is not confidence. There is not optimism. There is not a sense of hope. There is real despair.
The thing I find quite disappointing-in fact, it goes beyond disappointment; it becomes almost a question of amazement-is that a government brings in a budget and during the entire presentation and debate does not express the slightest iota of concern about the tens of thousands of people who have lost their jobs in the last four, five, six weeks. I do not know if somehow or other they live in constituencies where people are not losing jobs, but I do not hear any Conservative members talking about that problem.
The Minister of Finance, in his own paper, his own presentation, talks about a million and a half Canadians. And whenever he is questioned about that enormous

March 4, 1991
The Budget
figure, he says: "Well, it is not quite as bad as it was in 1981-82". But what he forgets to say is that the difference is that we are now dealing with a situation made specifically for Canada and not shared by other countries. Certainly, in 1981-82 we had a recession, but it was something that the entire world had to face. This is our own unique invention.
During the weekend in my constituency, people could not believe that with the recession now going apace, with every single statistical indicator showing a downturn, the only comfort is that the Minister of Finance says that it may get better a year from now, but there is nothing to offer any hope. Thlk to the small business people, Mr. Speaker, as I am sure you have. What do they tell you? Consumer spending is down 30 per cent, 40 per cent, 50 per cent. There is no question that there has been an enormous drop in consumer confidence and reaction.
In my riding there are stores that have been stable, well running businesses for years. They now have to go to their banks for new lines of credit and they are not sure that they will make it to the end of the year. Again, the budget is silent on this issue. There is not much in the way of sympathy, response or any kind of compassion for the undermining of that backbone of our economy, particularly when you consider that it has been self-induced. We have taken our own arsenic. As the shopkeepers in my riding tell me very clearly, it is a culmination of the recession but also the GST. We know that GST is pushing the inflation rate up; we have already seen the numbers.
But what is happening is that they are also beginning to see a serious unwillingness of people to buy. The psychology of it has become a major deterrent to engaging in the normal marketplace transactions. People are just staying at home or they are going across the border. They are heading south across the border to get the deals and sales, and all the other kinds of opportunities. I forget what the figures are, but I think it is about a 40 per cent increase of purchases in the United States in the last year or so. Again, the budget was silent on that issue: no care or concern.
In the last weeks my mailbox has been filled with letters from senior citizens who all of a sudden are realizing that the combination of Bill C-69, which started the capping of our social security program, is now
reaching a point where we are looking at a full scale federal pullout within a matter of five, six, seven years, depending on which province one is in. It is unacceptable for the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Health and Welfare, each day in this House, to try to camouflage and put up a smoke screen about what the meaning of that is.
We can talk about the transfer of tax points to the provinces that took place under the original funding of the EPF, but there was never any intention under that program to eliminate federal participation. As a result, the ability to have any kind of national system of education and health care now stands in jeopardy.
The Minister of Finance said today that he was going to put $28 and some odd billion in the next five years. Add that up. Look at the figures. In 1997, no more transfers at all to Ontario and Quebec, and the rest of the provinces by the year 2000. That means any ability to continue with national standards will have to be brought about, as the minister says, by special legislation which I am sure will be challenged constitutionally and probably thrown out of the courts. They know that. They are fully aware of that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope so.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope so. That is probably part of the game plan. That is part of the large devolutionist theory that we have been receiving from this government for so long.
We are not talking now about dollars and cents, we are talking about people, understanding that the very fundamental institutions on which they depended are now being dismantled.
Mr. Speaker, did you hear anywhere in the speech from the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Health and Welfare, acknowledging that this year there are over one million children living in poverty in Canada? And that we have one of the worst records of the western industrial world? I think that represents about 60 per cent of the cohort of children, compared to Norway or Sweden where it is about 5 per cent.
I just heard the Minister of Veterans Affairs say: "Hey, do not bother me with those kinds of spending programs". It is not a spending program we are talking about. We are talking about children. Close to 200,000
March 4, 1991

children go to food banks. We are talking about single parent families who are substantially dropping below the poverty line and cannot afford to maintain their rent or their housing any more.
The problem is that I do not think the Conservative government understands the basic and essential importance of a social contract in this country. We hear a lot about free enterprise and the market system from Conservative caucus members. But what they have never been quite able to understand is that the market system only works when there is an underlying base of social programs to give people some sense of security. There is a social contract in this country which we spent many years building up that underlies the operation and the entire economic system. If you begin to undermine the social contract, then you are going to undermine the market system along with it. They have never been able, in their ideology to understand that there is a clear, unmistakable integration and connection between maintaining a sense of security and stability amongst working people, seniors and young people. To allow them to participate in the market and to say: "I will take my chances and I will work around". Our whole attitude is, we turn it totally over to the private market system and then undermine the foundations upon which it is built.
That is part of the tragedy we face.
I would like to read from one of Canada's more insightful analysts, Michael Ignatieff, a brilliant writer who has looked at this question and the connection between them. He says that the whole basis, the establishment of an elaborate system of publicly supported social services, social integration and collective responsibility, becomes the hallmark of citizenship. He says that the whole idea of a social welfare state was intended to undergird formal legal rights with entitlements to social and economic security so that citizenship could become a real, as opposed to purely formal experience. Now we are seeing that basic social contract being ejected, being forgotten, in fact, deliberately being taken apart.
I suggest as a proposition, that any opportunity we have as a country to compete abroad, to deal with our problems, our interests on a national level, the kinds of stresses and strains we are facing, the lack of productivity, the increasing divergences between views from
The Budget
region to region, a large, contributing cause in the last six years has been the undermining of that social contract. That withering away of those rights of citizenship, the abandonment of the idea that individual citizens regardless of their money or their income or their place, could depend upon a certain basis of security.
If you take it away from them, of course they are going to react by drawing inwards, losing commitments, not being able to identify with the nation state called Canada. And it is hollow rhetoric for the Prime Minister to get up as he did a few weeks ago in his speech and say: "I am going to stand up for Canada". When, in fact, he and his government are clearly, deliberately, self-consciously taking apart the very fundamental ingredients that made this country work for many years.
Rather than building upon it, rather than recognizing that with free trade, with global competition and all the rest of it, you have to improve the social contract to give people a greater sense of security. In fact, we are taking it away.
Look what the budget does beyond that. We are now talking about further eliminations. The attack on the Public Service. I could see the cabinet sitting back and consulting with the great poll and saying oh, yes, public servants are not popular, let us go after them. Let us in effect eliminate collective bargaining in the Public Service. Let us dictate now what they will get and we will be the arbiters of what is fair or just and equal, to take away the whole notion of collective bargaining. And they say yes, people will see the screens and the angry faces and not pay attention. Again in my riding I have school teachers and nurses and social workers and air traffic controllers, public servants in Veterans Affairs. They are hard working, serious minded, contributing citizens of our country and they just had a right taken away, a fundamental right that is available to virtually everybody else. And it is done with impunity, indifference, no apology, not even saying we will try to find some way to make it fair. It just disappears. It is done with the kind of cynicism that they know. As one incumbent here says, almost to provoke a public strike if they can, as a basis of trying to improve popularity.
So once again we have a disappearance of one of those ingredients that made our society more civil, gave people a greater sense of commitment, a greater sense that they could be treated fairly.

March 4, 1991
The Budget
Public servants are not the culprits in this country, they are not responsible for the problems we get into. And yet at the same time that they are pointing their fingers and saying there is only going to be a 3 per cent cap and if you are going to go up to the 3 per cent cap you have to fire people to do it, this government has the gall to spend $179 million on a refugee board populated entirely with appointments of the government, most of them former candidates or something else, at $80,000 a year and they call that fairness.
When we left government, we spent $5 million on the refugee board. Five million, not $200 million and the same problems are being addressed and they had a report from their own committee in which their own members of the Commons addressed a solution that would have made it much easier, but no they had to do it their own way and their own way now costs taxpayers $179 million. I do not see that being cut back. I do not see that being restricted. I do not see the minister of employment saying I made one helluva mistake, I am going to go back to the drawing boards because all I am doing is paying for a bunch of Tory friends to get $80,000 a year plus expenses and may be more. And yet the refugee rolls grow larger and larger, the problem gets worse and worse and taxpayers spend more and more. I do not see that being hauled out as a sign of waste or duplication or inconsistency.
Oh, no. That is fair game. No one talks about that. I have not heard a Conservative member of Parliament yet mention that travesty. Why? Maybe they are hoping that sometime in the future they will get the same kind of perk. Instead, we zero in on the public servants.
Let me also, if I might, talk for a moment about the deficit. Everybody sort of says that the reason we are doing all this is that we have to deal with the deficit. I agree. The deficit is a serious issue, as much a serious issue for Liberals as it is for Tories. But the question is how do you respond to it.
Is it written somewhere in natural law that the only way you deal with a deficit is to cut back on social programs? Is it written that the only way to sort of bring the government fiscal framework into line is to cap programs for children, or education, or health care, or whatever?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is in the blue book.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It may be in
that little blue book that is carried around, but I will tell you. I do not hear anybody talking about the excesses of a capital gains system which gives vast amounts of money in write-offs to very, very wealthy Canadians. I do not hear them talking about the tax expenditures.
Even the Business Council on National Issues, perhaps the most devoted of Conservative friends in the country, has said openly: "Look, business gets hard to make grants and subsidies. We are giving away too much money. Cut it out".
I have seen nothing in this budget to do that, not one line of real change that is going on. But if we are talking about $6 billion or $7 billion of loopholes, of tax expenditures, surely a Minister of Finance who had some kind of imagination would have found that as an area in which to cut back, not the area of scarce social resources.
The fact of the matter is that when we look at the agenda index of countries we are in the lower percentile of industrial countries in our social spending, not in the upper percentile. But where we are sort of right up at the top is the kind of giveaways we offer. How many sort of big projects? I would say right now stop them, get rid of them, we do not need them any more. If we are looking for some answers let us look at things like real public investment in education, research, infrastructure in this country.
We do not need those kinds of major handouts any longer. I do not think they work any more. I fully expected, especially when many of the large corporate businesses are saying it is time to get rid of them, that they would have done so.
Finally, in budget terms, I want to spend just a moment talking about the fundamental issue that we have all been concerned about in this House, war and peace. Mr. Pearson once said that we prepare for war like bloated giants, and for peace like retarded pygmies. He must have had this budget in mind when he said it because we are quite prepared to substantially increase the cost of paying for a war, but when you get down to the question of whether we are prepared to pay for the damage of the war, the reconstruction in the Middle East, the environmental problems, what do we do? We cut back further on our ODA programs, make no offer of
March 4, 1991

any new assistance. We know what the problems are. We know that there are billions of dollars of reconstruction. We know that the Third World countries have had to pay excessive costs. I spoke to one ambassador of an African country just last week, $800 million have been taken out of their budget simply by the increase in oil prices.
But what does Canada do with all its rhetoric about how we are going to be a new international player, how we are going to build the peace? They cut back their commitments.
I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, you do not have peace if you do not have social and economic justice. You do not get social and economic justice when the disparity between rich and poor grows wider and wider. You are only going to eliminate that disparity when the industrial countries start making some serious commitments in how they overcome the gaps.
But there is nothing in this budget to show it. In fact it contradicts everything the minister of external affairs or the Prime Minister have said about their hopes for the future. The Minister of Finance has the real message of what this hope is, cutbacks, restraint, limitation, no commitments.
We are prepared to lecture everybody else about what they should do but when it comes down to really helping in a very concrete real way there is nothing on the table.
Mr. Speaker, I say to you let us look at the budget and the message it has. I thank you for your time and indulgence and I say to you that it was a time that Canadians were looking for some creative, imaginative, sympathetic, responsiveness to both the problems internally and domestically and all they got was the same old Michael Wilson.
