speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was listening with a great deal of interest to my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, talking about how the government might be able to do a better job in terms of its budgetary exercises. He mentioned a lot of what he called excesses in terms of government boards, commissions and so on.
The Budget
I have a couple of questions. First of all though, I might comment that I do notice that the hon. member takes his pay cheque home every week and with it, all of the expenses and perks that are accorded to all members of Parliament. I do not hear him suggesting that his own salary be cut.
He also says, as I mentioned before, boards, commissions and other political appointees should somehow be cut back, but he does not tell us how much that would total and how that would directly affect the deficit problem we have. Would that actually reduce our deficit significantly? He does not tell us about that because I think that he knows that in fact it would not, that it is really a very insignificant amount in terms of the over-all problem that we are dealing with.
He also refers to grants to businesses and suggests that it is time that the government cuts back on grants to business. Well, if he had read the budget or listened to the budget speech he would understand and he would remember that there was a promise of a $75 million cut of grants to businesses and other interest groups this coming year and another $125 million to follow that.
I would suggest that the government appreciates the hon. member's kind advice, but it has already tackled that issue in the budget that we have just heard a week ago.
Finally, the hon. member mentions that we can somehow get social and economic justice or suggests that somehow this government is lacking in providing a road map to social and economic justice, but the hon. member does not tell us how we are going to arrive at that goal by expanding the deficit and refusing to tackle the debt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that the member for Winnipeg South was able to come in for the last 20 per cent of my speech. Too bad she missed the first 80 per cent because many of those questions were already answered.
The first question was about members' salaries and perks. The last I heard the member was a member of the governing party. If that caucus had wanted to do it, they could have told the Minister of Finance and brought it in. We are not the government. So perhaps the member should answer the question herself because she is a member of the party that makes those decisions. If she wants to do that, then I give her full rein and licence to

March 4, 1991
The Budget
convince her colleagues to do it, and the Minister of Finance has the full opportunity to do it.
I do not write the budget. The hon. member for Winnipeg South helps write the budget and if she wants to make those voluntary, that is okay with me. But I will say to her, if she wants to go ahead and make voluntary reductions herself, I think we would be glad to hear it, if that is what she is prepared to do.
The fundamental issue is this, it is how you go about doing it. She said that we would like to make the right cuts. The point I was making is that the only language we hear from the Conservatives is cut payments to single parents, to children, to the health care system, to education. That is the problem. I gave her an example, $179 million for the refugee board. Well, there is a $100 million cut for job training, for the Jobs Strategy Program.
I will make a proposition. She and I will go together to the Minister of Finance and say, "Look, if you want to get rid of total waste, then cut your friends off all those boards, come up with a refugee program that works, take the $100 million and put it back into job training so we can put people back to work in this country, so that we can start training people who are being thrown out on the street, so we can provide them with some real understanding of what is real public investment."
The public investment in this country is not in a bunch of people who are making $80,000 on the refugee board, the real public investment would be to put people into training programs and to give them the skills they need rather than cutting $100 million of the program.
If the hon. member for Winnipeg South wants to do that, then let her stand up on her feet and say she is prepared to support the elimination of that board and its proper restructuring and to put the money where it really belongs, on people, to' help them get back to work and get the training they need. Those are the kinds of real decisions.
I will compliment the Minister of Finance totally on this. Thank God he had the sanity to stop the insanity of the Minister of Communications who was out doing institutes on cultural relations in Montreal and other places. At least someone got to him and put some sense of sanity back into his head.
But those are the kinds of extravagances, those are the kinds of excesses we are talking about and they are a legion under the Minister of Communications. We have not even begun to count up how many little pet projects he has been able to author. There is nothing wrong with the project itself if it creates something of value. If the government is really interested in helping the cultural community, recognizes its economic and social value, and puts money into it where it really works, then the artists will develop and expand their product and get their work performed. It is an important part of our society, but it is not the Thj Mahal that he wants to build. That is the problem, and those are the kinds of things that we are trying to raise.
There is a wonderful book by Sinclair Lewis called Elmer Gantry. It talks about a fundamentalist evangelical preacher who is always out-it reminds me very much of members on the other side- preaching about what is needed for salvation. Finally, someone came along and said: "That preacher is so busy telling us what is right, he forgets what is really good."
This is a government that is always preaching what is right and forgets what is really good.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member this question.
I was very intrigued to hear him speaking of excesses, extravagances and pet projects. We all know that when this member was a minister he was in that business himself in a particularly outstanding manner as it affected the community of Winnipeg.
Clearly members from Winnipeg would not want to raise this, but those of us in the rest of the west certainly were quite aware of the fact that when this member was minister he was quite deeply involved in extravagances and excesses in the city of Winnipeg. Nonetheless, I am delighted to see that the member has come around. I would just like to ask him one short question.
How many billions would you like to add to the deficit this year?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the observation of the member for Macleod just shows how this is a government that is unable to tell the difference between exaggeration and excess, like we have with the refugee board or a proper public investment as we made in Winnipeg, such as the Air Canada Computer Centre.
It provides a major technological advance for that city and provides employment for several hundred people as well as one of the most modem reservation systems in the country.
Is the member for Macleod saying that a major computer centre for an airline is an exaggeration? Is he saying that the investment in a major national research centre on industrial technology is an excess even though all westerners get to use it? It is the only way that small business in western Canada is able to undertake major improvements and innovations on industrial design.
Of course, the Tories would not think of that. No, they are much more interested in getting those old former Tory candidates on the Refugee Advisory Board. Now there is a sound investment. There is really good economics for you. Get your friends hired. That is how you really improve the economy of the country.
I want to come to the so-called simple question. The point I am making is that this government made no mention anywhere in its budget about the value of taking a look at a large number of those tax expenditures, the lack in the tax system that, for example, watches an orgy of takeovers, amalgamations and mergers because it does not tax that kind of foolish use of capital which totally undermines our economy.
It creates a paper economy which allows billions of dollars of capital to escape in this country to help buy companies in the United States or in other places and which adds no wealth to the country itself. That is the kind of real, I would hope, insight and real serious analysis that this government might some day try to make.
Frankly they will never get a chance because they will not be around that long.
The Budget

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On debate, the hon. member for Jonquiere.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the Budget Speech in this House on February 26, I suspected it might not contain very good news for the Canadian people. I think that is understandable, since, with interest rates around 10 percent, a debt or savings will double within a seven year period. That is what happened to us in Canada between 1984 and 1991. While the accumulated deficit we inherited when we came to power in 1984 was roughly $200 billion, it has now reached nearly $400 billion. This means enormous amounts must be expended from our Budget to service this debt.
For the current year, 1991-1992, the debt charges will total approximately $43 billion, which translates into $118 million a day for the taxpayers.
In this context, it is clear that any responsible Finance Minister from whatever government has no choice but to do his or her best to cut expenditures and try to avoid raising inflation. To improve our economic situation and get out of the recession, it is very tempting to increase expenditures. That would make a good impression. Theoretically, we could think that by increasing quickly our expenditures, we will increase employment and put the bad times behind us.
Allow me, to illustrate this point, to quote statistics from previous governments. Interest rates in 1981 stood at 22.75 per cent. As we speak today they are down to something like 10 per cent. Inflation in 1981 peaked at 12.7 per cent compared to roughly 5 per cent now. The unemployment rate in 1983, shortly before we took office, was 14 per cent, today it has gone down to about
10.5	to 10.9 per cent.
Of course we are aware of the current recession. We know that bankruptcies are on the rise throughout Canada-over 54,000 in the last year-and we can see that some people are having a hard time getting through.
So what options did we have in such a situation? I believe the Minister of Finance is steering the proper course under these circumstances. Among other things it is clear that the decision to freeze our expenditures or

March 4, 1991
The Budget
freeze the growth of our expenses at about 3 per cent until 1995 is an excellent option which should enable us to get a handle on inflation.
Mr. Speaker, you know that last year we chose to levy the goods and services tax and, from a political standpoint, that is not a paying proposition. There is no political return in implementing a 7 per cent tax on goods and services. Not one single Canadian is glad about or appreciates such decisions. But they were made by a responsible government that must take action not to become more popular or gather more votes but to administer a country which is experiencing trying times. We have to manage the country in such a way as to be able to pull ourselves out of the duldrums and control the debt.
Mr. Speaker, if we can control inflation and keep it down, by the same token we will lower interest rates and pave the way for future economic growth.
I would like to draw the attention of Canadians to some of the points in the Budget that I found particularly interesting. Perhaps I should explain, Mr. Speaker, that it would be very convenient for the government to decide that it could use the additional income from the Goods and Services Ikx to add new programs and take measures that are politically attractive. However, that is not what the government has done. It has decided to take the revenue from the GST and use it to reduce the deficit.
Another important point, and this is another innovation on the part of the government, is the decision to legislate spending limits. In other words, Mr. Speaker, if the government wants to set up a new program, it will have to respond to needs that did not exist before, and any programs that no longer respond to those new needs must first be removed, so that is another way in which this government has innovated and shown that it is serious about this Budget.
Of course, although I am a member of the Conservative Party, I am perfectly able to come out and say that I don't agree with everything in this Budget. It happens occasionally that members see things they do not particularly like, and for instance, as Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, and right in the middle of a recession, I would have preferred to see an increase in the budget for the
Canadian Job Strategy. However, the Minister of Finance decided otherwise, and the budget will be cut by $100 million.
On the face of it, this does not make sense, but we must see this as part of the general picture, as part of the unemployment insurance reform.
Mr. Speaker, you will recall that this Budget provides for nearly $500 million to be used for training workers this year. That amount will be added to the job strategy. The strategy's overall budget has varied between $1.5 and 1.6 billion annually since 1984. So now we have $500 million as a result of unemployment reform that will be added to the amount I just mentioned.
On the whole, Canadians will get more out of this Budget, even if, as far as the job strategy is concerned, there will be $100 million less. This week, during the Quebec caucus, I asked the responsible minister a number of questions to ensure that the regions will not be penalized as far as the strategy is concerned. On this basis, we have been assured by the Minister of Employment and Immigration that the various regions would not be affected. We will be in a position to provide more detailed information on this over the next few days.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I refer again to the $159 billion in expenditures, including $43 billion in debt servicing and $115 billion in programs spending. In view of such major budget, we have made a decision concerning the equalization payments to the provinces as well as the Established Programs Financing.
The provinces are always seeking a bigger share of the Federal government's tax revenues. However, we have to let the provinces know that they will have to administer their finances more wisely because we are compelled to make cuts. We just cannot impose such unpopular taxes as the GST and then give away the revenues to the provinces.
While dealing with equalization and transfer payments, I wish to remind the House that we are facing a Constitutional crisis and that, as such, they should be part of the forthcoming discussions with the provinces. I myself am a member of the joint committee currently visiting various parts of Canada to try and find solutions to the current Constitutional deadlock and I should like to emphasize that Constitutional problems are not likely to help putting the economy again on the right track.
March 4, 1991

We must live with that. We must tiy and find a way out of the deadlock. Together with my colleagues, I must find a way to remove the current Constitutional amending formula which requires unanimity. It is important, Mr. Speaker, for if we should fail, Canada would not survive. We must find a way to get rid of this straighjack-et which requires unanimity, so that Quebec may get some of the basic powers it needs, such as the protection of its language and culture, the appointment of judges to the Supreme Court, etc.
Of course, I refer to that in connection with the budget because indirectly these Constitutional problems have an impact of the budget of our country and they affect our economy. We want Canadians to realize that what is forthcoming is serious. If we can get rid of that unanimity provision I sincerely believe that Quebec will be able to sit again at the table and score some very crucial points concerning the protection of its language and culture, because unanimity will no longer be necessary. The new formula may require the support of seven provinces with at least 50 per cent of the population-this will have to be determined-but this is one of the assignments we are currently working on with my colleagues and the two co-chairmen, Senator Beaudoin and Mr. Edwards.
Mr. Speaker, I will not deal any further with this budget. We must keep in mind the two important measures concerning the GST. The money is there and the revenues will be used for debt reduction purposes. We also promise to pass legislation to limit the growth of our expenses, so that subsequent governments will pay as much attention as we do to efficient management of public funds.
I wish to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me the opportunity to participate in this debate. In conclusion, I would like to quote a couple of paragraphs from an article written by Mr. Frederic Wagniere, and published in La Presse. It says: "An Honest and Far-Seeing Budget. Michael Wilson tabled yesterday an honest budget which should answer many concerns expressed by Canadians. The Minister of Finance showed that the government understands how serious the economic and financial situation is in Canada and has decided to respond. The
The Budget
policies he is suggesting may seem simple, but that is not to say they will not be tough. You cannot hope to come out of a recession and reduce an enormous budget deficit without asking everyone to do his or her share. This Budget is simple insofar as it deals directly with problems and does not put our economic future in jeopardy."
I think this is an appropriate description of the responsible steps we have taken and will continue to take in order to control inflation and reach our goal of 2 percent by 1995. We also want interest rates to keep or going down as they have been doing since last May; they have dropped by 4 points. That is the direction we want to follow to allow our businesses to invest and our country to grow. We want to see the employment rate increase in every region in Canada and our people to do well.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the member from the government side, the member for Jonquiere, for his speech on the budget. I would like to pose a few questions to him.
He indicated that the interest rate in the 1980s rose to 22 per cent and today is at 10 per cent. Yet early this afternoon the finance minister indicated that the debt was not as substantial in the 1980s as it is today. We also heard that there has been a period of good economic growth since the election of 1984.
My question is: Who made the substantial debt today? It is obvious it is this government.
Then he spoke about not having any choice today. Well, he had a choice. The government had a choice in 1988, and that was to avoid the pre-election free spending that happened only to buy the votes of Canadians.
The member indicated that the income from the GST would help reduce the deficit. We have opposed the GST, but should revenue emanate from that and reduce the deficit it will, of course, be welcome. However, I would like to say he has forgotten the deficit of people, the basic needs for housing, shelter and education among the poor. Why will he not be prepared to consider reducing the deficit of people as well?

March 4, 1991
The Budget
Does the hon. member not make a distinction between deficit and investment? Deficit is when nothing comes out of it; expenditure on something that nothing good comes out of it, of course, is a deficit. But when you spend money for the future of our children, would he also call it a deficit? I would say it is an investment, to make them more competitive in the future.
He spoke about national unity. Would he agree that the strengthening and not the weakening of our social programs will be the national glue that will truly maintain the country? Also, would he agree that this budget will melt that glue?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his comments.
My answer to that, Mr. Speaker-and I want to repeat this because he may have been out of the House for that part of my remarks-is that if you have savings in the bank earning interest at about 10 per cent your money will double in seven years. The same thing happens if you are indebted: in seven years at an annual interest rate of about 10 per cent you will owe twice as much.
That is precisely what happened in Canada since 1984 when we took over and were confronted with a debt or a deficit amounting to $200 billion. Now it stands at $400 billion. These are the $400 billion which are costing you close to $43 billion in interest this year or, to put it another way, every day you are taking $118 million out of the pockets of Canadian taxpayers for interests alone.
I would point out to my colleague that when we took office in 1984 the government was spending $1.33 for every tax dollar collected. That is like spending more than you earn. At the time the government was giving Canadians $1.33 worth of services for every dollar it was taking in.
With that in mind you can understand that one simply cannot erase the debt overnight. That is not possible. There is no way we can rise tomorrow morning and say that the $30.5 billion deficit we had the night before-as we will have for 1991-92-has been reduced to zero. What a crisis we would have on our hands! We have to act more responsibly and more reasonably just so that gradually we can manage to bring our program expenditures in line with our revenues and eventually regain
control and reduce the $400-odd billion debt we are carrying now.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since nobody wants to seize the opportunity, I cannot let it pass.
In his reply, the hon. member said that perhaps I was not here. I never left my seat. I was listening intently and, of course, I was disappointed in his analysis. That was the problem and he has to admit that.
With respect to the question of spending of the capital and the interest, the fact remains that we have had good economic growth over the last six years and this government has not been able to decrease the deficit. Now it says "You cannot eliminate it overnight." Well, it has had six years. It is not overnight. I think he is trying to defend a defenceless position. I think he has to admit that the government has lost credibility and does not have the capability to hold on the deficit and it must resign so that we can have a new mandate and lead Canadians to greater prosperity.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to welcome all of those who are watching here this afternoon to what I will call "Parliamentary Pursuit". If you think you have the answer, I want you to bang the table as hard as you can, and the first one gets to answer the question.
Are we all set? Are all the Tories ready? Are all my colleagues behind me ready? Are all those Liberals over there ready?
Here is the question: Who was selected by Euromoney magazine as "The World's Worst Finance Minister"? I will give you three choices: (a) Michael Wilson of Canada; (b) Otto Stich of Switzerland; or (c) Li Peng of China?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Michael Wilson.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear the name Michael Wilson. I want to tell you that if you had picked all three, you would have been correct. These are the three worst finance ministers in the world.
Poor old Li Peng has been retired for recycling, so he does not have his job any more. But Otto Stich, who led Switzerland into stagflation, is still holding on to his spot. And we still have Michael Wilson as finance minister.
What was it that qualified him for this award as the worst finance minister in the world? Look at the accomplishments. In two years, this finance minister has made projections. He made projections on the deficit, and he was wrong. He made projections on the inflation rate, and he was wrong. He made projections on the unemployment rate, and he was wrong. He made projections on the interest rates, and he was wrong. He was wrong, wrong, wrong, wrong. This is the wrong minister in the wrong government at the wrong time in the wrong country.
The Budget
Look at the accomplishments. Can you believe this? This is a real accomplishment. Here we are in the middle of a recession. It was started as a made-in-Canada recession. We have a recession and we also have high inflation. So, we have an inflationary recession. This is quite an accomplishment.
The other day I saw a very interesting movie, Edward Scissorhands. After seeing that movie and reading the budget, I came to the conclusion that what we have here is Michael Scissorhands. Now, for those who have not seen this move, Michael Scissorhands is a character whose hands were all scissors. At first, Michael was loved by the community because he could cut the hedges in interesting ways, he could cut your hair in interesting ways and everybody loved him. But, there was an unfortunate thing. Even in this beauty of cutting and cutting and cutting, he inflicted some scars on himself. He cut himself.
Then something happened to Michael Scissorhands, he fell in love. Is that not marvellous. Nothing that we can attribute to our own finance minister, but Edward Scissorhands fell in love. Unfortunately he was used. The story goes on that he was used by tfie boyfriend of the girl he fell in love with. Then poor Michael Scissorhands, unfortunately, had to return to his castle in the sky. Have I got the story more or less right?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
So it was cut, cut, cut and, eventually, he went up to his fictional palace in the sky.
I look at our own finance minister and I ask: "How is Michael Scissorhands like that?" I mean, look at what he has done. He started out cutting, cutting, cutting and cutting. I would suggest that his cuts are really putting slashes on the body corporate of our country.
Tories are groaning, Mr. Speaker, but it is fact. Now, let's go through the budget. Let us take a look at what the Conservatives, under the present regime, are projecting as economic nirvana. Notice that all of these projections are going to happen after 1993. We know what is going to happen. That is an E-year, and all of these things will be in Tory heaven. If this is an example of Tory hell, can you imagine what Tbry heaven is like? All of this economic nirvana will come after 1993.

March 4, 1991
The Budget
Tory heaven is a place where there will be have an average of 2.2 per cent inflation, not 3 per cent and not 4 per cent, but 2.2 per cent. Tory heaven is going to be a competitive place. Tory heaven is going to be a place where people will have to become predators to survive. It will be a place where unemployment will be 10 per cent or more on average. It is a place where the federal government is going to transfer the responsibility for the erosion of social programs to the provinces. It is a place where the wages earned in this country are going to be wages of fear and insecurity. It is a place where in their struggle to keep their share of shrinking government funds, provinces are going to be pitted against provinces, workers are going to be pitted against workers. It is a place where the government's main function will be efficiency and not public service.
Michael Scissorhands, the Minister of Finance for Canada's corporate welfare state, is promising that nirvana to Canadians. It will all, he says, happen in 1993, after the election.
Under the Liberals, we saw them turn Canada, our country, into a corporate servant. These Tories are turning Canada into a corporate slave. We have seen all the tools of public policy gradually captured by Bay Street and the BCNI. Why is it that in all of this budget it is working people, it is the working poor, it is the working middle-class who are making all the contributions to the attack on the deficit? Why is Michael Scissorhands being used by his friends? That is the similarity with the Edward Scissorhands movie. He is being used by the corporate sector.
Look at the projections for corporate profits in 1993. Look at the corporate profits and where they are going. This minister, Michael Scissorhands, did not lay scissors on the corporate sector; not one pair of scissors was laid on the corporate sector, not one.
I think the people in my riding and the people across the country asked the question: "I do not mind making a contribution to bringing the deficit down, but why do I have to make a total sacrifice? Where is the contribution from the corporate sector which gets so much out of this economy? Why aren't they making a contribution?"
These are the new functions of Michael Scissorhands' corporate welfare state. The government's sole role shall
be to enforce the laws of the marketplace as interpreted by the BCNI. They are to use the power of the budget and interest rates to implement the corporate agenda.
I think that we have been misled. This is a shell game. When we have been thinking all along that the government really was out to fight the deficit and the debt and that everybody was focused on that, I think the real agenda was to put in place what I call the corporate agenda; in fact to put in place certain processes, certain laws to remove the government from any interference in the marketplace, so that in fact this market can deal with all the problems of Canada.
While we are focusing on fighting the government on the debt and the deficit, very quietly it is putting in place the other part of the more important agenda. It is putting in place, for example, deregulation. It is putting in place privatization. It entered into a free trade agreement.
Anything that enters us into and locks us into a continental agreement, whether it is energy, whether it is trade, the fact of the matter is whatever government takes office would find it very, very difficult to extricate itself.
These stories can go to their reward knowing full well that nobody-no socialist government, no Liberal government, no whatever other government after-can interfere with the agenda that it has achieved for its friends.
What are the new functions of the corporate welfare state? Cut budget expenditures and subject the people of Canada to artificial scarcity. Michael Scissorhands sends a clear signal to financial markets that the value of their future earnings is safe.
Look at what else they tell us. We have to be competitive. In other words, we have to dampen the demand of workers for a fair share of the wealth that they produce, so workers should take a buck an hour because we have to compete with Thiwan or we have to compete with Mexico or any other country that does not offer their workers the same benefits for their labour that we offer in this country and for which many of them fought over many years to establish or to win.
I have never seen a sumo wrestler corporation having been built up by this government. I have never seen any

of them out of the goodness of their heart-I have got to correct that. That is not true. The Blue Jays just gave Dave Stieb a nice big increase and he did not ask for it. Of course, there is no collective bargaining there. There is only arbitration. I have never seen it.
I ask the member from Westmount, if he has ever experience a corporation that came along and said to the workers: "Oh, you have done a great job. What this government is doing is establishing certain criteria for the corporate welfare state, that is to cut wages and Canadian purchasing power.
The next thing they want to do as part of that agenda is to cut the Public Service force and replace them with Revenue Canada arm-twisters, so they can get more taxes out of them, collect more GST, and so we move away from public servants who actually serve people to ones who are going to take money out of their pockets. That is what we see. Look at the work force to collect the GST. That is expanding, that is expanding.
It seems to me that this government is changing the nature of government so that people will have a good reason to hate it. All that we have seen Michael Scissorhands do is cut, cut, cut.
Now the Tories say: "Brothers repent, salvation is at hand". What is salvation to attain Tory heaven? What is salvation to attain this Tory heaven? I hear somebody say: "What is it?" I will tell you since you asked. It says salvation will come through international trade, international trade. We have to be globally competitive. Have you not heard that? Salvation is there.
What do we have to do? The middle class and working poor in this country must go on a diet so that in fact we cut the social programs and we raise the taxes. What we have to do is we have to build those of our corporations that can compete internationally. In other words, we have to develop sumo wrestlers. No Hulk Hogans for this government; salvation rests with developing sumo wrestlers, because it is these sumo wrestlers who will provide us entry into the Tory nirvana.

But these sumo wrestlers are never satisfied. They always want more and more and more. They are always saying to their lackeys in government, the Tories, run up, run up. Doc, I have the spot here for you, right here.
What have they done? They have turned over government. They have built up the power of these international corporations that have got to go out and compete for us.
So I ask: What is inflationary and what is not? If workers get an increase beyond 3 per cent, that is inflationary. That is inflationary. Here are some figures. Why are these not inflationary? I also want to mention to the hon. member that the sumo wrestler class in Japanese history was there to protect those who were unable to protect themselves. Perhaps the hon. member's analogy is an appropriate one because obviously if we do not have good corporate citizens to produce well we will not have the wealth we need to protect people who are less capable of looking after themselves.
I must commend the hon. member on for once in his life making a little bit of sense in his fine analogy about sumo wrestlers. We do need protection for people who cannot look after themselves in this society and the Conservative government certainly understands and recognizes that. That is why its budgetary measures have been so appropriate to the needs of the people who are underprivileged and who really do need a helping hand once in a while.
I also want to mention that we heard a lot about how the NDP would somehow turn around this problem that we have in Canada vis-a-vis our deficit. In fact, in terms of my own experience with the NDP which is a long one in the province of Manitoba, I do not see anything to support that.
For example, when the NDP was in government for many years in Manitoba they turned the province into a virtual corporate desert. There are very few of the major corporate offices still in existence in Manitoba which we at one time enjoyed because they were taxed out of existence through the very strange sort of economic policies of the NDP when they were in power.
I do not quite understand how the hon. member would suggest to us that NDP policies would somehow cure the ills of Canada, that by taxing corporations we would somehow generate more wealth to spend on the people who really do need help.
I suggest that the hon. member has a veiy twisted view of how economics work in this country, or in any country indeed in the world.
In fact, we know that the NDP does not believe in the deficit. It thinks that if we owe money to ourselves

therefore no deficit exists and no debt exists. That is not exactly the way the rest of the world views the situation.
Also the hon. member talks about nirvana. Nirvana, he says, is something that this government strives for through using budgetary measures, which I suggest will probably have a very profound effect in getting us to nirvana if we are given enough time and opportunity to let our measures take effect.
We do know that the NDP idea of nirvana is something that you get to by spending other people's money. The NDP never understands that you have to generate wealth by doing something productive, by manufacturing things, by making a little wealth, by making a profit. That is the way to generate the kind of wealth that can then be used to create the kind of Utopian kind of society we hear about all the time from members like the hon. member opposite.
I would suggest that when hon. member talks about nirvana he has a very short-sighted idea of how to get there. He would get there by spending my money, your money, the money of the taxpayers of this country, for his ideas rather than what is really necessary and good for the corporate body of the country.
Finally, I wonder whether members of NDP would tell us where they base their wonderful projections, on what experience? Do they base it on the experience of Russia, communist Russia, socialist Russia? Perhaps they base their economic theories on the wonderful experience of communist China, socialist China. Oh, no, I am sure they are going to hold up the example of Sweden, that great social democratic society which has just introduced a goods and services type tax at 24 per cent and which is in terrible trouble.
I do not know where members of the NDP are getting their secret plans for the future of this country, but perhaps the hon. member would take a moment to share with us just on what he bases his profound conviction that they have the right economic policies and plans for the country.
He talks about recession. I do not want to take all the time here, but he suggests that somehow the rich do well out of recession. I wonder if the member would tell me just who benefits when interest rates come down. That is one the effects of recession. Perhaps he would share some of his wisdom with us.

Mr. Speaker, first of all let me say to the member that I have never lived in Manitoba. I do not know the political history and all the ramifications in Manitoba, but I can tell her of a province that I know, a province where history is unfolding, and that is the province of Ontario.
The Ontario government took over with a deficit. The Ontario government had choices to make. One of the choices it made was that it was not going to reduce any deficits on the backs of the working people of the province of Ontario. It made the choice that it was not going to cut back the services to the people of the province of Ontario. People pay for services and they are those services such as health care, education and social assistance that we cannot cut back. There are services that people are entitled to such as child care.
I used poor old Edward Scissorhands, who was a lovable character in the movie. What I tried to characterize with Edward Scissorhands is an unlovable character of Michael Scissorhands, the finance minister of this country. The sumo wrestlers in the present context certainly do not have that philosophy of protection any more. We have changed that image of sumo wrestlers, in terms of corporations being compared to them, in the fact that they want to get bigger, larger and heavier so that they could in fact compete in their class. That is the comparison.
Now we get to the corporations. If I look at the projections in the budget on page 44, I see the projections in the Thble 2 of incomes. Real personal disposable income is projected in 1992 to go up 1.3 per cent. Corporate profits before taxes will go up 29.1 per cent. Already the revenues collected from corporations have been declining as compared to revenues collected from individual Canadians.
What we have been arguing with this government about is that there ought to be some fairness. If you are going to wage a war on reducing the deficit and the debt, fine, but there has to be an element of fairness. In other words, if you are asking ordinary, average, middle income Canadians and the working poor to bear the brunt of reducing the deficit, they ought to be able to look at examples of where the corporate sector is bearing its fair share of reducing the deficit.
We on this side of the House said: "Look, how do you think this deficit kept increasing?" It is because this

government followed a high interest rate policy. Why? Because John Crow said there were fires of inflation.
Where were the fires of inflation? The fires of inflation were not in Alberta. They certainly were not in Atlantic Canada. They were not in northern Ontario. Those fires of inflation were in Toronto. To diffuse the fires of inflation in Toronto we followed this government.
This government followed a high interest rate policy. For every 1 per cent the interest rate went up, the deficit went up $2 billion. We kept saying to the government that it ought not be following this policy.
Many others in this country said: "You ought not be following this policy." The fact of the matter is that the government brought on this recession. We are in the middle of a recession. What do you have the government doing? Slashing and cutting. Michael Scissorhands is at work cutting and cutting. This is not the time to cut.
We should be spending money. She asked how we would deal with this. I say to the minister that we would deal with this question. Where is the money that we put into research and development? If anything at all, down the road ought to be able to put us in a competitive world position.
There is no money being spent on research and development. There are cutbacks. We are spending less than the other industrialized nations as a per cent of our GDP on research and development.
The government is cutting back on post-secondary education so what we are going to hand down to future generations of Canadians are post-secondary institutions that are falling apart. Programs have been raped and destroyed, so I say to the hon. member: You are wrong, wrong, wrong and the course you are following now is still wrong.

Our plan for economic development takes a different path. Its goal is not only to end the recession but to restore strong, continuing growth that leads to renewed prosperity. This path is the more difficult one at present but I firmly believe that the finance minister has made the right choices at this time.
As the minister outlined in his budget speech, the key to recovery is lower interest rates. This will be achieved through concrete actions which he outlined for us. First, clear achievable inflation targets issued jointly by the Governor of the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance to reduce inflation to 2 per cent by the end of 1995. Second, government finances will be put firmly on course to a balanced budget. The existing expenditure control plan introduced last year will be extended and backed up with legislated program spending limits. All revenues from the goods and services tax and privatization will flow into the Debt Servicing and Reduction Fund, something which Canadians have been crying for for a long time. Third, and very important, the operating costs of government including wages and salaries will be severely restrained.
As well, a number of recent expenditure decisions have been reconsidered, such as the previously announced contribution of $88 million to the Toronto ballet and opera house; there is the provision of financial support for the construction of concert halls in Edmonton and Montreal; and just recently the cultural research institute in Montreal. In my riding these limitations have been widely applauded at this time of severe financial restraint.
It is important also to note that we are not asking anyone else to do something which we as a government are not willing to do ourselves. We will be setting an example by reducing our own spending. Starting right at the top, the Prime Minister and the cabinet ministers will be taking a pay freeze this year. New restrictions will be put also on the members of Parliament during this coming year.
Government departments will have to absorb any wage increases within the existing budgets. The government
The Budget
will also be eliminating layers of bureaucratic management and reduce the number of senior managers by 10 per cent. Again, this is something which people have been asking for in Canada for a long time.
As a result of these very concrete policies, key fiscal goals will be achieved. The Canadian economy will recover in the latter half of this year. Over-all we recognize that there will be a 1 per cent shrinkage in 1991 or this year, but it will rebound next year with a 3.5 per cent growth, a tremendous improvement and certainly something that we are anticipating very much.
New federal borrowing in financial markets will be eliminated in 1993-94. This is going to be a day of great celebration for all Canadians. Program spending growth will be limited to an average of 3 per cent per year after 1991-92. The deficit will be held to $30.5 billion this year and next despite the effects of the recession in this country. In 1992-93 with recovery and lower interest rates, the deficit will fall below $25 billion for the first time in a decade, a real accomplishment with all the various programs that have been assisted and developed.
The budget will result in a better balance between fiscal and monetary policy and this will provide the lower interest rates and greater confidence essential to economic recovery. At the same time, the budget reflects sensitivity to current economic difficulties. In other words, in spite of all the number crunching, we have not forgotten the human factor, the people who have lost their jobs, the elderly, the farmers who are struggling due to problems beyond their control in the global market.
In 1991-92, we will increase program spending by 6.9 per cent. My personal preference would be to see no increase, but we recognize again, in these difficult times, that there are people out there who definitely need help. This will mean a total increase in spending of $7.5 billion, which will be spent when it is needed and, indeed, where it is needed. Of this, $3 billion will be going for assistance to the unemployed, $1.6 billion to the elderly, and $1.3 billion to help our farmers.
In addition, our defence spending was increased by $600 million to help with increased responsibilities we are all aware of in the Middle East situation. Of these

four areas, these will account for 80 per cent of the increase in our program spending.
As well, exemptions will be continued for income support programs for seniors, for families and veterans, unemployment insurance, as well as the equalization program and the Canada Assistance Plan payments to lower income provinces.
Again, a very important point, that Indian and Inuit programs will also be exempted as will defence spending. These programs account for 60 per cent of program spending and will grow at an average rate of 3.9 per cent from 1991-92 to 1995-96.
All other program spending will grow at an average annual rate of 1.7 per cent.
This budget, of course, also contains important new tax measures to benefit the disabled. These measures constitute just one element of the government strategy to promote equal opportunities for Canadians with disabilities. They build on an impressive series of initiatives to improve the quality of life of Canadians with disabilities and remove the barriers to their full participation in our society.
For example, the government has, first of all, appointed a minister responsible for the status of disabled persons. It has passed the Employment Equity Act to promote the hiring of Canadians with disabilities. It has broadened the eligibility for the disability tax credit while increasing its value and providing for greater transferability to family members.
There have been increased Canada Pension Plan disability benefits. The new measure announced on Tbesday will have a value of $70 million a year to Canada's disabled and their families. As part of the new measures, the disability tax credit will be raised from $575 to $700 annually.
The definition of expenses eligible for the medical expense tax credit will be broadened. This will now include the cost of part-time attendants in the home. We recognize how essential it is to give families relief from the constant care of those who are severely disabled. It will also allow for specially trained service animals such as seeing eye dogs, modifications to the home, widening doorways, this type of thing, and incontinence products which, as we know, are tremendously expensive and, up
until this stage, have been a severe burden on those disabled who required them.
Also, any costs that are acquired by employers in modifying their places of work to accommodate disabled persons are fully deductible in the year in which they are incurred. Allowances provided to employees for taxi fares, Para Transport and parking will no longer be considered as taxable benefits.
Having a disability is no longer a reason to be kept out of the mainstream. By assisting both the employees and the employers, these new tax measures will help ensure that disabled Canadians have equal opportunities to participate in the workforce.
As I stated at the beginning of my remarks, I believe that the measures being taken in this budget will lead our nation forward to continuing growth and renewed prosperity. We must plan for the long-term.
Many of my constituents have written to me, they have phoned me, they have stopped me on the street and very frequently they compare the nation's finances to their own household finances and they say, "You just use common sense, spend only what you can afford. Set a budget and stick with it. Do not live on credit." I firmly agree with these remarks and, I think, as a government, we are beginning to see this developing.
That is why I am pleased that future program spending will be managed tightly and expenditure limits on program spending will be imposed by legislation for the next five years. This will allow Canadians further assurance that their money is being spent wisely. These limits will be set in law to ensure that the budget's program spending track will be met. This law will be a significant and a welcome change to the way the government manages its expenditures.
I am pleased that the budget will address public concerns that revenues from the goods and services tax might be used to finance new spending instead of reducing the deficit. Time after time I have people come up and talk to me and say: "The only reason you guys want more money is so that you can spend it somewhere else." So, I am veiy pleased that that we can assure them that all of the revenue from the goods and services tax will be used to reduce the debt and indeed the deficit.
This will be done through legislation, to establish the Debt Servicing and Reduction Fund, into which all GST revenues will flow, as well as privatization revenues and contributions from individuals and businesses. I am sure

we have all had constituents who have come to us and offered money to help reduce the government debt because of their deep concern for what it is doing to their country.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to read into the record a letter written in November, 1990 by Richard C. Halverson, Chaplain of the United States Senate. Mr. Halverson wrote:
Dear Friend:
In my ten years as Chaplain of the Senate, I cannot remember a time of greater frustration among members of Congress and their staffs, or more expressions of anger from the people.
Several years ago, there came to my attention a quote from the book written by Alexander Fraser Tytler. Mr. Tytler lived at the end of the 18th century and the early part of the 19th. He wrote a book entitled The Decline and Fall of the Athenian Republic.
Amazing, is it not, that the following quotation from that book, written about an ancient democracy, long before American democracy had really been tested, is so timely.
Mr. Tytler wrote:
A democracy cannot exist as a permanent form of government. It
can only exist until the voters discover that they can vote themselves
money from the Public Treasury.
And I think that is a very significant factor in our discussion today.
From that moment on the majority always votes for the candidates promising the most benefits from the Public Treasury with a result that a democracy always collapses over loose fiscal policy followed by a dictatorship. The average of the world's great civilizations has been 200 years. These nations have progressed through the following sequence -
And I would just remind hon. members that this was written 200 years ago. The sequence is:
From bondage to spiritual faith; from spiritual faith to great courage; from courage to liberty; from liberty to abundance; from abundance to selfishness; from selfishness to complacency; from complacency to apathy; from apathy to dependency; from dependency back into bondage.
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest today that if we are to keep Canada out of bondage, if we are to keep the Canada of the future free, if our children, our grandchildren, our great grandchildren and beyond are to enjoy the freedom and the quality of life that we enjoy today, we must do the honest thing, we must do that which is right and live within our means today, rather than mortgaging and placing into bondage future generations of Canadians. I believe that this budget is just one more step in the return to fiscal responsibility demanded by thoughtful Canadians everywhere, and it is the only way
The Budget
to maintain the good things that we all appreciate so very much.

March 4, 1991
The Budget
a separate set of books for it, and all that silly nonsense is nothing more than a fraud on the taxpayers of Canada. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member very much for that important and probing question. By the time the next election comes around and the spendthrifts would seek office again, the citizens of Canada will say: "Hey, we did not like it at the time, but these guys really knew what they were doing and they stuck to it even though people did not accept it."

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a comment and a question. I first want to congratulate my colleague from Delta on a solid and substantial contribution, a good common sense contribution to this debate and one that was most necessary.
It is quite evident to virtually every Canadian that the problem we face today is one which built up through the 1970s and indeed, through the 1980s, as a result of consistent government failure to take in enough revenue to cover programs and the continual shortfall. The deficits added up to the national debt we have today and the requirement to service that debt, to pay interest on it, which today is consuming something in the order of 35 to 38 cents out of every revenue dollar that comes in. Well, it is quite clear that leave perhaps 65 cents or less out of every revenue dollar to provide the services and the programs that Canadians have come to expect. Small wonder they are upset.
The problem is that for a number of years, through the 1970s and the early 1980s, perhaps Canadians were getting, whether they wanted it or not, $1.20 to $1.25 worth of government largess for every dollar of tax revenue that was contributed. The difference, of course, was being funded through endless borrowing. The credit card has run out. The spending has reached its limit.
March 4, 1991

What I am hearing from opposition members by way of criticism now is that somehow government today should ignore the realities, should ignore the experiences of the 1970s and the 1980s and continue to borrow more. Somehow we are supposed to go out and borrow even more money so that even more of the government's taxation revenue will be taken up in service charges, in paying interest on government debt.
In Question Period today, an opposition member said: "Let's get real". I just heard an opposition member suggesting that the caring and compassionate provincial government in Ontario was going to, undoubtedly, run up a huge deficit, and in doing so would not be looking after the problems of today on the backs of ordinary Canadians, or words to that effect.
I would like to ask my colleague from Delta, in light of past experience, how on earth can spending more and borrowing more today, be helpful. How in the world could that attitude be helpful, given the experience of the past.
