The Budget

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his budget speech, the Minister of Finance, quite understandably, tried to make the case that there is no alternative to the government's economic policies. It is the government's way or the profligate spending of the opposition, just as had been suggested by the speaker who preceded me. It is this question which I wish to explore, namely, is there an alternative to the government's policy?
We, in our party, share the view of many Canadians that the federal fiscal deficit is a serious economic and political problem. Our leader notably did not make a single spending commitment in the leadership campaign last year. And I know that in the election campaign, which will come up in a year or two, he will present to Canadians a program that is fiscally responsible.
So we agree that the federal fiscal deficit is a problem. We also agree that achieving low levels of inflation is an important objective. There is no disagreement with these objectives.
The first question we must ask ourselves then is what is the government's record with respect to these objectives? The inflation rate today exceeds 7 per cent, compared with less than 4 per cent when the Conservatives first took office. The deficit is forecast to be $30.5 billion, which is $2 billion higher than the deficit forecast in last year's budget. Contrast this with the statement of the finance minister in his first budget in May 1985 that he would reduce the deficit by the end of the decade to $18 billion. He missed the mark by the small sum of $12.5 billion.
It is precisely because of the government's failure to achieve its objectives that many Canadians are having increasing doubts about the ability of the government of the Conservatives to manage the economy.
Our responsibility as an opposition is to remind Canadians that this government has failed to achieve its objectives to reduce the deficit and to control inflation and to suggest where the government may have erred.
To reduce the deficit, an appropriate balance is required between reduced expenditures, increased taxes and economic growth. It is generally recognized that the government did not do enough to cut spending in the years where the country enjoyed reasonably strong growth. On the contrary, the government relied heavily on tax increases. For example, in the April 1989 budget,

March 4, 1991
The Budget
of the $9 billion in deficit-reducing measures introduced for the fiscal year 1990-91, $7.2 billion or four-fifths were tax increases and only $1.9 billion or one-fifth were spending cuts. It was these very tax increases that contributed to inflation.
In its 1990 Annual Report, the Economic Council of Canada observes:
The main source of upward momentum in the rate of inflation since mid-1989 has been regulated prices, especially in the service sector. Included in this category are prices that are directly influenced by federal, provincial and municipal policies. The largest increases since early 1989 have affected gasoline prices, vehicle registration fees, tobacco and alcohol, public transportation and water rates.
In short, by persistently raising sales taxes, the federal government has been directly responsible for much of the inflation we are experiencing today in Canada.
A further point. Doug Peters, Vice-President and Chief Economist of the Toronto-Dominion Bank has also explained how monetary policy, rather than reducing inflation, has caused fiscal policy to increase inflation. As monetary policy tightens, as interest rates rise, fiscal policy eases and the deficit rises because of increased interest payments. In sum, high interest rates contributed to inflation and, of course, high interest rates have greatly increased the debt and the deficit.
Yet, despite this abysmal record, the government, in this budget, tells Canadians that it is staying the course with the policies that have failed so miserably in the past. The finance minister proposes to keep real interest rates at the historically high levels that we have seen in recent years.
On page 52 of the budget, Mr. Speaker, and I invite you to read this, the finance minister says that in the medium term, that is through 1996, and I quote:
The real interest rate-the nominal rate adjusted for inflation-is expected to average about 4-3/4 per cent. This is similar to the average of the 1980s and about three percentage points higher than the average of the 1960s and-1970s.
It seems obvious to me, if it is not obvious to the finance minister and to the members of the Conservative party, that with real interest rates of 4.75 per cent we will not get the deficit down. This is not only because such high real rates increase interest on the debt, but because it will be impossible for the economy to grow with interest rates that high.
We must recognize that the whole budgetary policy of the government is premised on high economic growth, led by exports. High growth is required for the government to meet its deficit targets, reduce unemployment and raise living standards.
But nothing in the budget will promote that. Have Canadian exporters not been telling us that they cannot compete with the dollar at 88 cents U.S.? Yet the government says that it will keep the dollar at 88 cents U.S. by maintaining high real interest rates. How are we going to get increased exports? How are we going to get export-led economic growth?
It is time to recognize that the government has failed to achieve the objectives it has set for itself, namely reducing the deficit and controlling inflation.
To summarize the reasons for this failure: One, it failed to cut spending when it had the opportunity to do so; two, it relied far too heavily on tax increases, which in themselves were inflationary; three, monetary policy has been too tight, which has also contributed to inflation and the growing debt; and, four, tax increases, high interest rates and the high dollar have hurt our ability to compete and strangled exports.
Is there an alternative to this approach? That was the question I asked at the outset.

In its most recent annual review, the Economic Council of Canada explains that price stability should not be the only economic objective of the Bank of Canada and the government. There should be two objectives: price stability and full employment, and three means: a monetary and fiscal policy and a labour force policy.
According to the Council, if there is a lesson to be learned from the 80's economic policies, it is that fighting inflation exclusively through the monetary policy is very costly.
The Council emphasizes the experience of a number of European countries that have succeeded for close to twenty years in defeating inflation without creating unemployment.
The Council says there is no magic formula. However, those countries have certain things in common. First,
March 4, 1991

they committed themselves to full employment. Second, governments, employers and unions work hand in hand. The Council thinks it would be possible in Canada to co-ordinate better the economic policies of the federal and provincial governments and to bring employers and unions closer together. The Council's recommendations, I suggest, offer an alternative to the present policies of the Conservative government.
Mr. Speaker, it bears repeating that the Council has found in a number of European countries a commitment to full lemployment. That is particularly significant for us, Canadians. This government seems to be resigned to high unemployment. Indeed, he predicts an unemployment rate of 10 percent for this year and of 9.8 percent for next year.
I want to add a few words on the particular position of Montreal. The biggest concentration of unemployed in Canada is in Montreal, Mr. Speaker. They are 207 000 this year compared to 169 000 last year. And unemployment and poverty cannot be dissociated. Montreal has become the Canadian capital of the poor. There is more poor in Montreal than in all of the Atlantic Provinces combined, Mr. Speaker. It was recently said of Montreal, which was quite striking, that it is no longer possible to talk of it in terms of pockets of poverty but in terms of pockets of wealth since the whole city has become poor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is true.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What I am saying, Mr. Speaker, is that we must deal with the plague of poverty and the plague of unemployment. So let us add full employment to our economic objectives as suggested by the Economic Council of Canada. Obviously, the conservative budget completely disregards that recommendation of the Council.
In the budget, the finance minister announced that the government will "launch a national effort to build a new partnership for prosperity". He said: "As a first step, the government will release a discussion paper in the spring to help focus public debate about the problems we face and to try to develop solutions".
The Budget
Mr. Speaker, you will forgive me if I say that these words ring rather hollow. It is now seven years since the Prime Minister made his commitment to double Canada's R and D effort by the end of the first mandate. He made that commitment in a speech to the Chambre de commerce in Montreal in March 1984 when he was Leader of the Opposition.
It is now seven years since that speech when, again, he committed to double Canada's R and D effort by the end of the first mandate.
As well, we remember the Prime Minister's words in his book, Where I Stand. He said: "Research and development and the resulting innovations are the lifeblood of a successful economy and country". The Prime Minister asserted that if the percentage of Gross Domestic Product allocated to research and development were increased by just 1 per cent, we would create in Canada one million jobs and $20 billion in additional sales of manufactured products.
In an effort to protect consumers, I suggest the publisher of the Prime Minister's book change the title to Where I Stood. That is because we know what has happened since 1984. The government talks a good game. It has introduced with much fanfare a number of high profile initiatives, but let us look at the other side of the ledger.
Total support for Canada's research and development efforts have actually declined, and I want to highlight a number of examples. First, the Conservative government has reduced support for research and development in industry. For example, highly successful procurement programs have been cancelled and the National Research Council's Industrial Research Assistance Program has been starved for funds.
This is the same program which is perhaps the most highly touted government program. It was even recommended by the Nielsen report for its effectiveness. It has been starved for funds.
Second, the government has cut transfer payments for post-secondary education and reduced over-all funding for vocational training.
Third, the government has decimated Canada's premier research organization, the National Research Council, and cut funding for government based research on the environment and alternative energy.

March 4, 1991
The Budget
Fourth, it has cut the staff of the Science Council of Canada by half.
Fifth, with respect to university research, the government established the Centres of Excellence program but at the same time froze funding for the main sources of university research in Canada, the Federal Granting Council. It has ignored the recommendations of the Prime Minister's own blue ribbon committee, a committee which he chairs and announced with much fanfare several years ago.
He has ignored the recommendations of his own National Advisory Board on Science and Technology to double the funding to these granting councils.
Sixth, applied health care research is the last area to be cut by the Conservatives. This includes research into preventive health care, health promotion, disease prevention, workplace hazards and cancer prevention.
The government seems to have forgotten the old adage that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. They tell us that health care costs are rising too quickly. At the very same time, they cut funds for applied health care research and research into health promotion and preventive health care.
What is the bottom line of all these actions? It is the internationally recognized indicator of scientific activity that the Prime Minister referred to, namely the percentage of Gross Domestic Product allocated to research and development. Such spending in Canada has actually gone down since the government took office from close to 1.4 per cent of our Gross Domestic Product to 1.3 per cent of Gross Domestic Product.
The Prime Minister seems to have forgotten what he said in his book, Where I Stand, that just a 1 per cent increase in research and development spending would create in Canada one million jobs and $20 billion in additional sales of manufactured products. That percentage of scientific activity has gone down by 1 per cent, not gone up, not doubled as the Prime Minister promised in his speech in March 1984. This is at the same time that our major competitors continue to invest twice as much as we do in comparative terms and are increasing their spending.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Short-sighted promises.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We come back to the budget in which the Minister of Finance says that more needs to be done to assure our future prosperity. I quote from the minister's speech again: "We need to look hard at the quality of our investments in infrastructure, machinery and equipment, training and education, and research and technology". "There are signs," he said, "that in some areas, such as private sector spending on training and research we are not doing enough".
My reaction on reading the budget was, this is news to the Minister of Finance. For years, members of Parliament have heard from countless sources that we are falling behind in all these areas. From university teachers, university presidents, from students, from high school teachers, from business executives and workers, from union leaders, from the government's own advisory committees, the case has been made consistently and eloquently. Seven years after this government took office, it proposes to focus public debate on these issues.
Where has the government been for the past seven years? Has it not been the government's responsibility to take action in these areas, to show leadership, to do something about it? The debate the government proposes to engage Canadians now in is an admission of failure, an admission that we have lost seven years when this government should have taken steps to ensure that all Canadians receive quality education and that Canadians businesses do enough R and D. On the contrary, we have seen that all of their actions have defeated those very purposes.
On the very first page of his budget speech the Minister of Finance said:
-we must deal with the world as it is, and not as we might wish it to be.
I have two comments to make about this. Again, it is now almost seven years since this government took office. It is responsible for the world as it is. The Canada of today is what it is in part because of the actions of this government. It is time, therefore, that the government assumed responsibility for the difficult economic circumstances we are experiencing in Canada today.
Second, when I heard the finance minister say, "We must deal with the world as it is", I could not help thinking that Bobby Kennedy put it somewhat differently. He said, as if we need to be reminded, that "Some
March 4, 1991

people see things as they are and ask why. I dream things that never were and ask why not". What a contrast. When the finance minister of Canada says to Canadians is: "Don't dream, don't be ambitious, accept the world as it is with all of the calamities that this government has visited upon you".
Liberals have a different view of things. We believe that we can build a better world. We believe that we can build a better Canada. Canadians believe that collectively we can build a better world and a better Canada. This is what we should be setting our sights on doing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to my hon. friend and indeed appreciate the position that he put. I think all Canadians would wish for more funds for education, more funds for R and D, and indeed more funds for many worth-while causes. 1 do not think anyone would seriously quarrel with those suggestions.
What I would like to ask my hon. friend is: How can we manage to achieve these things, given the mountain of debt that we have and the requirement to pay interest on it? There is no use going back into the why and the cause of that. We know what the amount was in the spring of 1985, at the end of the last fiscal year of the previous Liberal government, and we know the effects of compound interest on that.
The fact is that interest has to be paid on it and, to the extent that it is, it takes away from the ability of any government to have the funds necessary for those other things which we would all like to have.
The hon. member refers to dreams. It is good to have those and it is good to have wishes, but we cannot simply wish away the debt and we cannot wish away the requirement to pay interest on it.
In order to fund all these things that the hon. member would like to have, what other programs would he cut out and, if he is not going to cut out any programs and reduce spending at all, what increases would he bring forward by way of taxes? What tax measures would he introduce in order to be able to find the funds necessary?
The Budget

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. He asks me how we would provide more funds for education and research and development, how we would find these funds.
I find it somewhat perplexing that a member of the government is asking a member of the opposition how to find more funds for education and research and development.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: With a straight face too.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
With a straight face, as my colleague reminds me. It seems to me that this government should have some ideas about how we could find funds for education and research and development or how we could stimulate the private sector to put more money into training.
While I am on it, there was the de Grandpre commission which had to look into the question of adjustment to the free trade agreement and made a whole number of recommendations which this government have ignored. If he wants to find some answers, he might look at some of the recommendations of the de Grandpre commission.
I would like to suggest to the member that he was not listening really to my speech, because in it I said that to reduce the deficit we need a balanced approach which combines spending cuts, tax increases and economic growth. This government seems to have forgotten that one way to reduce the deficit is to make the country grow. I want to put it to him that the budget tabled in this House last week by the Minister of Finance will not accomplish those objectives.
I would like to read to him from a budget analysis prepared by the Toronto-Dominion Bank, Department of Economic Research: "The main problem of this budget is that it addresses none of Canada's major economic problems. Spending cuts and major tax increases such as the 25 per cent rise in unemployment insurance premiums for both business and employees will not only prolong this recession but will themselves defeat Mr. Wilson's deficit reduction objectives".
What I am saying to the member is that it is time that he and the members of his party and the Minister of Finance owned up to their failure to achieve the objectives that they set for Canadians, namely to reduce the deficit and the debt and to control inflation.

The Budget

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker mentioned that there were three ways of dealing with the deficit: cutting spending, increasing taxes, and stimulating growth. I would not disagree with those but I think he has missed a couple of very, very critical ones. One, is stopping the tax loopholes for the large corporations, the tax concessions which are a major part of the reason we are into debt.
If the Tory government has not reduced the tax load for its friends, had not left the loopholes that the Liberals had put in place, there would be substantial reduction in the debt.
Also the member forgot to mention interest rates. My calculations are if there was a 4 per cent difference in interest rates on $400 billion that would be a saving of $16 billion right there.
I would like the member to comment on those two additional areas, the fiscal policy of this government that I think is responsible for a large percentage of the current deficit, and what steps they need to take to ensure that we are not simply compounding it with continued high interest rate policy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the member who I believe is a member of the New Democratic Party, if I am not mistaken-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, he is.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-talks about stopping tax loopholes. It is really remarkable how the NDP talks out of both sides of the mouth on this question. They say that they are interested in promoting economic growth, yet rail against tax incentives which have as their purpose to encourage businesses to invest in research and development, or training of workers, or capital investments of one kind or another.
I do not think the member recognizes or remembers that this government has indeed cut out some tax incentives which stimulated economic growth. Several years ago they passed a law which, for all intents and purposes, meant that companies that invest in R and D could no longer deduct the cost of buildings in which they do their research for tax purposes.
Can you imagine that, Mr. Speaker? A company has got to do research and development and they have a lot of sophisticated equipment, computers, et cetera, and they cannot put them anywhere because the Income Tax Act which the Conservative government has passed does
not allow them to claim an expense for the building that they have to have this equipment in.
I remember the reaction of Jean de Grandpre who, at the time, was president of Bell Canada Enterprises which is the parent company of perhaps Canada's only multinational company doing world-class research, namely Northern Telecom and Bell Northern Research. He said that this tax change initiated by the Conservative government would result in Northern Telecom doing research in the United States. This is exactly what is happening.
Is that the kind of tax loophole that the member for the NDP wants to see eliminated?
I get the impression from listening to the New Democratic Party that they want the Conservative government to continue cutting tax incentives which would stimulate economic growth and provide jobs to Canadians. It would seem to me that one of these days they have to fish or cut bait and tell Canadians where exactly they stand on these questions.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Resuming debate. The hon. member for Abitibi.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this budget debate. To begin with, I would like to say concerning transfer payments, that the federal government is trying to increase its control over its own program spending. It is not always easy. For instance, the Canada Assistance Plan is administered by the provinces as long as they satisfy certain conditions. The federal government has to match the provinces' contributions, and has consequently no control over these outlays.
One of the things we noticed in this year's federal budget is that Val-d'Or, in Abitibi-Temiscamingue, will be the site of a research centre called CANMET. No one has ever seen liberal members, nor the NDP, or members of the Bloc Quebecois-members from the province of Quebec-try to obtain the establishment of such a mining research center in the province of Quebec.
What has been done these last few years, especially the last two? It is with the help of economic and political representatives of our region, like the development corporation, CERDAT and the mining association of Quebec that we won the battle. I am proud of it because
March 4, 1991

this project will bring 15 million to the region over 5 years, starting this year.
Mr. Speaker, the spending control plan announced in last year's budget will be extended for the next three years. The Prime Minister's salary as well as that of all Cabinet ministers will be frozen. New limits-limits only-will be imposed on the salaries of the members of Parliament and senators. As far as I am concerned, they could have been frozen as well, I would have been glad to oblige.
Mr. Speaker, we bandy about a lot of figures. In all the speeches we heard, everyone, in the government as well as in the opposition, threw in a bunch of figures on the budget. I would like to tell the Canadian people, and more particularly the Quebec people, what I have done to try and reduce my expenditures as a member of Parliament. Often, in Abitibi, we attend social functions with senior citizens or young people who tell us how we should cut expenditures in Parliament. As we know, they total about $240 million for this House and another $40 million for the other place. Tonight, my speech is directed at all members of Parliament: conservatives, liberals, NDPers and members from the Bloc Quebecois. I guess we could call it, as the members from the Bloc Quebecois would say, a non-partisan speech.
Before issuing this release following the presentation of the Estimates on February 26, 1990, I had communicated some information to the media and said that, I for one, would be ready to restrict my privileges as member of Parliament. Members of Parliament are entitled to four free householder mailings a year to their riding. I checked what could be saved by applying mainly the restrictions imposed in 1990 by the hon. Robert de Cotret on the printing of the documents for such mailings, when he was the President of the Treasury Board, but the saving was insignificant.
For example, in 1989, I mailed a 44-page calendar which cost $9,000 for printing alone. Preparation and photomechanical reproduction costed $1,000 and mailing through Canada Post, $2,500. The total cost of this householder mailing to my riding was $12,400. Following the February 20, 1990 Budget, I had told a radio announcer from Radio-Nord, in Val-d'Or, that the Minister of Finance of Canada should, among other things, cut the number of free householder mailings
The Budget
Federal members of Parliament are allowed to make from four to a one only a year. The savings to the Canadian people would be $8.8 million if all conservative, liberal and new-democrat members joined in this effort. Personally, as a Conservative member from a northern riding, I decided to inform my constituents that I would send only one householder a year, not because I don't feel like sending four, but I say we have to cut expenses. People are told they have to pay taxes, and the government is cutting programs. For instance, at the time they cut a program that enabled students to travel across Canada. I told my constituents I was going to cut down to one householder and that I would no longer be sending 2,000 Christmas cards every year, and there would be no more birthday cards for my constituents. My message was: The government is asking Canadians to tighten their belts. I think it is only fair that as the federal member for Abitibi, I should cut my own spending and set an example for my constituents.
In May 1990, a new directive was issued concerning our 64 points for travel in Canada. We have a points system. Instead of money, we have a certain number of points for travel to our ridings. A directive issued by a committee said that spouses would be allowed the same number of points to go anywhere in Canada. That was one of the privileges, and I immediately objected. I wrote to the Speaker of the House of Commons, Mr. Fraser, and he said the following:
I understand that this new provision will help ease some of the professional and family pressures on members. In the case of large ridings without easy access, members and spouses will be able to travel more readily and more frequently within their province, while formerly such trips were designated as special travel.
That is one of the measures to which I objected. However, to show my constituents what my expenses were as a member, I told them in a statement in the House of Commons on November 22 1990, about my travel expenses in the riding of Abitibi, which is quite considerable and covers 554,000 square kilometres, from September 1984 to March 31, 1990:
-my travelling expenses in Abitibi and elsewhere in Canada amounted to $180,804, or $32,382 a year on average.
If I had applied all 64 points within my riding, to go to the northern part of the riding, it would have cost me $2,500 each trip, or $160,000 a year. I refer also to householder mailings, how much it cost me since 1984,

March 4, 1991
The Budget
for 26 mailings: $155,000. And I explained how I proceeded to send my Christmas wishes to my constituents, by making a statement in the House of Commons, for a saving of $15,000.
On December 12, 1990,1 wrote to the Speaker of the House of Commons asking him to change the Members' Manual of Allowances and Services. I wrote:
There is no doubt that Canada is going through difficult economic times and it is essential to ensure good management of the expenses in the House of Commons as well as in Canada.
We must take measures to reduce substantially the expenses (privileges) of the federal Members of Parliament in Canada and to cut by 20 per cent the estimates of the House of Commons in Ottawa for 1991-92.
We all know that for several months budget cuts and even total cuts have been made which have affected various programs and caused difficulties to many organizations.
The example I was referring to earlier:
(student exchange programs, women's issues, etc.)
Since the federal government is committed to spending restraint, members must do their share even if this creates some difficulties.
I know that some changes have been made already but I think sincerely that more can be done, including in allowances and services to members.
My suggestions to the Speaker of the House of Commons were the following:
The system of the 64 travelling points allowed to members. Each member is allowed, by periods of 12 consecutive months, a total of 64 points which he or she can use as follows:
I suggested to come back to the old system and not give the 64 points at large, which means across Canada. I told the Speaker: "Let us come back to the old system and keep the 64 points directly for the return trips to constituencies."
Allocate 15 of the 64 points to dependent children for return trips between the constituency and Ottawa.
Allocate 9 of the 64 points to his or her staff for return trips between the constituency and Ottawa.
2) Special trips
Members can use 20 of these 64 points for return trips between Ottawa and the constituency or any other destination in Canada for a direct flight with short stops to the destination city (which means that they cannot have several stopovers on their way there, except in case of emergency).

Members who want that some of their relatives enjoy those travel as provided by the 64 point-system can do so by designating one of the following categories to that end: children (son, daughter), parents (mother, father)
And most of all, I wanted to do away with the designation of all other family members and the printing of householder mailings; I wanted to substitute the following for Chapter F-3 of the Members's Manual of Allowances and Services, that is, the printing of only four householder mailings and/or letters, foldout format brochures, postal cards, questionnaires be allowed to be mailed within the riding of the hon. member, that such four householder mailings be printed and sent at the rate of one (1) every three months for a total of four mailings a year to prevent the sending of two or three newsletters the same month.
Concerning another chapter on printing, I proposed to allow the mailing of only 10 per cent of a householder within the riding of a member.
As for Christmas and New Year greetings containing a message from Parliament, instead of allowing the printing 2,000 cards, I proposed to limit that number to 500, and that any overrun be applied against the member's budget.
In a letter to Speaker Fraser about stationary and office supplies, I said that quotas should be applied on all stationary and desk supplies, as of January 1 1991, and that once these quotas were used, any requisition for stationary or office supplies would be charged against the Main Estimates after a review by the Board of Internal Economy of the House of Commons (quota for the office of members of the House of Commons).
Financial reports to members: That the travel summary-64 points system-mention the travel costs for each trip and that it be cumulative. One other thing: That the funds allocated to subsidies and contributions to parliamentary associations and delegations be further reduced by 10 percent each year in 1990-91,1991-92 and 1992-93. All members should coordinate their efforts towards such a reduction for a period of three (3) years.
I have received a response to my letter dated December 13 to Mr. Speaker, who always answers to me promptly, and here is what it says: "I want to thank you for your letter and your suggestions concerning some modifications to be made to the Members' Manual of
March 4, 1991

Allowances and Services in order to reduce the House of Commons expenditures. The Board members studied your proposals and agreed to ask members of the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services to examine them and to give their comments and recommendations." That was back in December, but since that time, I did not receive anything from the Committee on Privileges and Elections. It has been silent. I did not receive any letter from that committee.
I have a really important thing to say: when I started examining that matter, Mr. Speaker, what I really liked was that, immediately after Tbesday December 18, Bill C-79 was tabled before the House of Commons and one of its clauses that many of us are aware of read: Disclosure of expenditures. After thoughtful discussion, the committee recommended a more detailed disclosure of expenditures directly related to members of Parliament. Canadians are entitled to know just how elected MPs spend their tax dollars.
In a spirit of financial openness and transparency we will therefore have to tell the public what use we make of these funds. However the committee is still not sure what is the best way to proceed. What is known is that we will have to strike a proper balance between the principle of financial transparency and the principle of parliamentary independence. The information has to be sufficiently detailed, but not to the point of losing sight of the basic issue. We will also have to respect the right to privacy of the employees and the privileges of hon. members. We ought to give serious consideration to every facet of the release of these data and to the procedural aspects of the discussions.
Mr. Speaker, on January 11 of this year 19911 held a press conference in my riding and told local media representatives that I, Guy Saint-Julien, Member of Parliament, will make public all expenses incurred in 1991 in the discharge of my parliamentary duties, including my privileges as a member.
I said that I had tabled a letter in the House of Commons, that I had told the Speaker that I would make a quarterly report to my constituents so that indeed Canadians and Quebecers would know about all my
The Budget
privileges, that is all the expenses for my Ottawa office and my riding offices, and all the expenses incurred for my work as a Member of Parliament such as parliamentary travels, travels as member of parliamentary associations or parliamentary and government delegations, trips paid for by Canadian or foreign promoters and all the expenses allowed by my privileges; I would disclose them every three months, four times a year to my constituents. I wanted to take these steps for the purpose of reducing the many privileges granted to hon. members, as I did last year after Michael Wilson tabled his Budget on February 20, 1990. I said in my statement:
It is essential for him to control expenditures out of public funds, in view of the Federal Government's sustained commitment to limit its expenditures in departments, Crown corporations, programs, etc.
Abitibi men and women have the right to know how their elected representative spends the money they give him.
In a spirit of financial openness and transparency, following the tabling by Hon. Marcel Danis on December 18, 1990 of the Sixth Report of the Special Committee responsible for looking into Bill C-79 on the Parliament of Canada which deals for instance with the disclosure of expenditures.
That is what I had decided to do for my constituents a long time before last week's budget.
I wrote to the Speaker to know how I could find out about all my expenses both in this place and in the Senate. I asked the Speaker concerning the production of an expenditure report:
The Comptroller of the House advises me that he is not in a position to provide such financial information as requested in your letter.
Beside the expenses incurred directly by your offices (Ottawa and riding), the House of Commons is not responsible for keeping data about the various costs of each hon. member. Translation expenses are paid by the Secretary of State without going through the House. Likewise, most of telecommunication costs paid by the House are provided to all hon. members. It would be impossible, therefore, to provide you with the total expenses incurred by your offices, or to ensure their correctness, because organizations outside of Parliament pay some of these costs.
Then he referred to the Act of Parliament and so on and so forth. I still continue my efforts with a view to finding a way to obtain data concerning all my expenses which I want to disclose every quarterly to my Abitibi constituents.

March 4, 1991
The Budget
There is another point I would like to make, Mr. Speaker which is not mentioned in the Budget. It concerns mostly one of the issues contained in bill C-79, that is, the joint services offered to both Houses.
While examining the House of Commons administrative machinery, the committee realized that there is a lot of duplication between both Houses. Most services this House needs are also needed by the Senate. The committee believes that we could save public funds if we rationalized administrative services with a view to a better coordination. The committee however recognizes the importance of safeguarding the independence of each House. Within the scope of its proceedings, the committee will discuss the process needed to ensure consideration of these matters.
Mr. Speaker, before January 30, I wrote to the chairman of the Committee who had this to answer:
I appreciate your interest in the proceedings of the Special Committee on the Review of the Parliament of Canada Act.
He added:
Unfortunately, I cannot give you a list of joint services offered to both Houses. I do not know if such a list exists. For more information, I suggest you write to the Administrator of the House of Commons, Mr. Ed Riedel, or the Clerk of the Senate, Mr. Gordon L. Barnhart. Both of these gentlemen or at least one of them should be able to provide you with a complete list of these services.
Finally, members of this Committee seem convinced that better coordination of services offered to both Houses would improve our administrative efficiency. However, our Committee did not look into this matter in detail; instead, we called upon the experience and knowledge of our members and personnel.
I see, Mr. Speaker, you are telling me I have two minutes left. One more point about joint services. I went to the basement once to buy some stamps and I stopped at the wrong counter. I was at the Senate post office. As a member of this House, I do have to buy my own stamps in order to pay my bills. They would not let me buy stamps. They told me I was at the wrong counter, to go to the members post office. If we were to combine these two services in one, we would save money. Messengers of both Houses, production, publications, maintenance, cleaning, security, translation, distribution, postal service, general works, purchasing branch, transportation, nobody can produce a list, but I just did. I have given you the list. That is where we should save. We would save millions of dollars. If all those services were put together, we could save maybe $20 million between the two Houses.
I am pleased I have one minute left, Mr. Speaker. I wrote the two persons concerned and asked one thing. On February 19, I wrote the Speaker the following:
-I ask that a joint committee be struck as soon as possible to establish a joint administration of both Houses for the services they have in common -
And so on, all the services I will mention to you.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude in saying that I acted that way because I felt it was important. The people of Canada, the people from my constituency are told to tighten their belts. Companies, since a few months, are cutting their expenses, and wherever they can, they are imposing quotas. My speech tonight, a non partisan speech, contained two points to remember, namely the quarterly publication of members' expenses, starting in 1991 and continuing in the following years, and then a joint committee, of the House of Commons and the Senate, to coordinate the services of these two houses, thereby allowing savings of public funds.
I hope that all the members have understood my message.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments. The hon. member for Saint-Leonard.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see that my colleague is very keen on cutting expenditures. I am sure that his suggestions will be studied by the various committees, like the Management and Members' Services Committee and the Board of Internal Economy.
However, Mr. Speaker, I would like to address the budget, because that is what we are debating today. I would like to ask my colleague from Abitibi, who is so keen on cuts, whether he did the same exercise with the government and its Estimates. The Estimates, tabled two days after the budget, show $3 billion spending for the government, including advertising, public relations and the like. Three billion dollars. At a time when we are asking Canadians to cut on health care, when we increase unemployment insurance premiums, when we cut on housing for the homeless and on education, it seems to me that we could have cut in these three billon for advertising.
So, I was wondering whether the hon. member for Abitibi also wrote to the Minister of Finance to ask him to do something about that. Mr. Speaker, rich or poor, you don't know when you are going to require health care. When you are sick, you are sick. So, if you curtail health care for the poor, you should also be able to curtail the advertising budget of the government. Millions of dollars are being spent on promoting the GST and on a number of other programs.
March 4, 1991

So, for all that, I will leave time to my colleague in order that he can answer. I know there are a few minutes left, but it is time any way, Mr. Speaker. If the government claims that cuts must be made, if it begs everybody to tighten one's belt, it must not do it at the expense of the needy, but rather begin by doing it to itself. I know the government needs advertising since it is so low in the opinion polls, but I am under the impression that even if it doubled the sum it spends on advertising, that is $6 billions instead of the $3 billions now available, it would not be better off, since the government itself is finished. So, maybe it could cut the $3 billions in advertising expenditures. That would allow it to reduce the debt of an amount of $3 billions and would leave untouched the social programs which are necessary for the poor.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Abitibi has one minute and a half left.
Mr. Speaker, it will be a pleasure to respond in one minute and a half. I knew he would not ask any questions about what I said.
Do all members of the Quebec caucus agree with you?

I will let you speak if you want to. About members from Quebec, I said what I had to say quite frankly. You do not even have the courage to ask me questions about what I said in my speech.
The hon. member asked me questions about cuts in publications. He should start by doing that himself in his constituency. As I said earlier, I did it in my riding: householders were cut from four to one. I want to say that I already wrote to Treasury Board about that. All members receive in their offices nice glossy brochures from Petro-Canada, nice colourful folders from government departments, et cetera. I wrote to Treasury Board to ask them to do as they do in Quebec, in two colours, with the Quebec flag and the Canadian flag. But you did not dare-
